Opening# Today# Your group problems; 2. Simple linear regression: least squares; 3. How much to trust the result: SE, \(t\), \(R^2\); 4. Multiple linear regression; the normal equations; 5. Qualitative inputs and interactions; 6. Curves that become straight lines; 7. Gradient descent The plan. Items 2–6 are ISLP Sections 3.1–3.3. Item 7 is not in ISLP; it is the method used to train models that have no formula, and we meet it here on the simplest possible case.
Reading: ISLP Chapter 3 (3.1–3.3). ESL Chapter 3 (3.1–3.2) for the mathematics
ISLP explains the ideas with little mathematics. ESL Sections 3.1–3.2 give the matrix derivations of the normal equations and of the standard errors.
Notebook: lecture02_linear_regression.ipynb on Google Classroom
It computes every number on these slides and asks questions about them.
From last week: your group problems# Part Linear regression Representation a straight line (or plane) Evaluation sum of squared errors Optimisation a formula, or gradient descent Every ML method has three parts. For linear regression: representation — a straight line (or plane); evaluation — sum of squared errors; optimisation — a formula, or gradient descent
Lecture 1 described every ML method by three choices. Linear regression is the simplest example of each: the model family is all straight lines (or planes, with several inputs); a line is scored by the sum of its squared errors; and the best line is found either exactly by a formula (slides 9 and 18) or step by step by gradient descent (slides 25–29).
Group presentations (15 minutes): one minute per group: the problem your group will solve. What is \(X\)? What is \(Y\)? Regression or classification? Where will the data come from? The class critiques each choice
Each group states its project problem in the language of Lecture 1: the inputs \(X\) (what is measured), the output \(Y\) (what is predicted), whether \(Y\) is a number (regression) or a category (classification), and where the data will come from. Other groups question each choice.
Try it: Keep strictly to one minute per group. Note problems where the data source is unclear; those groups need to find data first (slide 32).
Words used all through today# Word or symbol Meaning Example (sensor) \(X\) (input) what we measure and use to predict reference temperature \(Y\) (output) what we want to predict sensor voltage data point one measured example (also: observation, reading) one reading \(i\) numbers the data points: \(i = 1, 2, \dots, n\) reading number \(i\) \(n\) how many data points we have \(n = 20\) \(x_i\), \(y_i\) input and output of data point \(i\) temperature and voltage of reading \(i\) This lecture is the first with real formulas, and the same few words and letters appear on almost every slide from now on. Students who skipped Lecture 1, or who learnt statistics with other notation, should meet them once, with an example, before they are used. Go through the table quickly, pointing at the sensor column.
\(X\) (input): what we measure and use to predict; example: reference temperature
Also called a predictor, a feature or an independent variable. In the calibration, the temperature read from a trusted reference thermometer.
\(Y\) (output): what we want to predict; example: sensor voltage
Also called the response, target or dependent variable.
Data point: one measured example (also: observation, reading); example: one reading
One row of the data table: one temperature and the voltage measured at it.
\(i\): numbers the data points, \(i = 1, 2, \dots, n\); \(n\): how many data points we have, \(n = 20\)
\(i\) is a label, not a quantity: reading 1, reading 2, and so on.
\(x_i\), \(y_i\): input and output of data point \(i\)
\(x_7\) is the temperature of the seventh reading and \(y_7\) its voltage.
Capital \(X\), \(Y\): the quantities in general. Small \(x_i\), \(y_i\): one particular measured value
“\(Y\) rises with \(X\)” is a statement about temperature and voltage in general; “\(y_7 = 380\) mV” is one number in the table.
Three marks on symbols: hat, bar and sum# Mark Meaning Example hat: \(\hat y\) predicted or estimated from data \(\hat y_i\) = the voltage our line predicts for reading \(i\) bar: \(\bar x\) the average \(\bar x = (x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_n)/n\) sum: \(\sum_i\) add up over all data points \(\sum_i x_i = x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_n\) Hat: \(\hat y\): predicted or estimated from data; example: \(\hat y_i\) = the voltage our line predicts for reading \(i\)
The hat is the most important mark of the course. \(y_i\) is what was measured; \(\hat y_i\) is what the model says. Their difference is the error the model makes on that point. A hat on a coefficient, \(\hat\beta_1\), means the value estimated from our data, as opposed to the unknown true value \(\beta_1\).
Bar: \(\bar x\): the average; \(\bar x = (x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_n)/n\)
Pronounced “x bar”.
Sum: \(\sum_i\): add up over all data points; \(\sum_i x_i = x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_n\)
The capital Greek letter sigma, written large. The \(i\) underneath says what is being counted.
Example with 3 numbers: \(x_1 = 2\), \(x_2 = 4\), \(x_3 = 9\): \(\sum_i x_i = 2 + 4 + 9 = 15\); \(\bar x = 15/3 = 5\)
Try it: Ask a student to compute \(\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)\) for these numbers: \((-3) + (-1) + 4 = 0\). Deviations from the average always add up to zero, which is why the formulas square them.

title: Opening
content:
Opening# Today# Your group datasets; 2. Logistic regression; 3. Fitting by maximum likelihood; 4. The confusion matrix, the threshold and the ROC curve; 5. LDA, QDA and naive Bayes; 6. Comparing classifiers on test data Items 2–3 are ISLP 4.3; item 4 is ISLP 4.4.2 (Table 4.4 and Figure 4.8); item 5 is ISLP 4.4; item 6 is ISLP 4.5. KNN was introduced in Lecture 1 and returns in the comparison.
Reading: ISLP Chapter 4 (4.1–4.5). ESL Chapter 4 (4.1–4.4) for the mathematics
ESL 4.3 derives LDA and QDA; ESL 4.4 derives the fitting of logistic regression.
Notebook: lecture03_classification.ipynb on Google Classroom
It computes every number on the slides and asks ten questions.
From last week: your group datasets# Last week the output \(Y\) was a number. Today \(Y\) is a category: \(Y = 1\) yes (e.g. faulty), \(Y = 0\) no (e.g. healthy)
With two classes we code the output as 0 or 1. Which class is called 1 is our choice; usually the one we want to detect.
We want the probability that \(Y = 1\): \(p(X) = \Pr(Y = 1 \mid X)\)
Rather than a bare yes/no answer, we estimate a probability.
The vertical bar is new notation for many students. The probability changes with the inputs: a motor vibrating at 6 mm/s has a different probability of a fault from one at 2 mm/s.
Group check (10 minutes): each group, one sentence on the dataset you found. How many rows? Which columns? Is your \(Y\) a number or a category?
Last week each group was asked to find a dataset. This is a quick check that every group has one, and that they know whether their problem is regression (Lecture 2) or classification (today).
Try it: Note any group without data; they must have one before Lecture 4.
Symbols
\(Y\) Output: 1 or 0. \(p(X)\) Probability that \(Y = 1\) for inputs \(X\). \(\Pr(A \mid B)\) Probability of \(A\) given \(B\). Words from Lectures 1 and 2 that we use today# Word Meaning coefficient \(\beta\) a number the model learns from the data hat: \(\hat p\), \(\hat\beta\) predicted or estimated from data loss, cost \(J\) loss: error on one point; cost: average loss over all points gradient descent reduce the cost step by step: \(\bb \leftarrow \bb - \alpha\nabla J\), with step size \(\alpha\) standard error (SE) the “\(\pm\)” of an estimate: how much it would change with new data training / test data data used to fit the model / new data used only to judge it standardise \(z = (x - \bar x)/s\): mean 0, spread 1 KNN \(K\)-nearest neighbours: predict the most common class of the \(K\) closest training points Today's lecture leans on words from the first two lectures. Students who missed a class, or are not yet fluent with them, should not meet them again without a definition. Go through the table quickly, with one example each.
Coefficient \(\beta\): a number the model learns from the data. Hat: \(\hat p\), \(\hat\beta\): predicted or estimated from data
Today the coefficients sit inside a sigmoid, but they are still found from the data, and a hat still marks an estimate.
Loss, cost \(J\): loss: error on one point; cost: average loss over all points
Lecture 2 used the squared error. Today the loss changes to the cross-entropy (slide 13); the idea of averaging it into a cost does not.
Gradient descent: reduce the cost step by step, \(\bb \leftarrow \bb - \alpha\nabla J\), with step size \(\alpha\)
Logistic regression has no formula for the best coefficients, so gradient descent is now essential, not optional.
Standard error (SE): the “\(\pm\)” of an estimate: how much it would change with new data
Used on slide 15 for the motors.
Training / test data: data used to fit the model / new data used only to judge it
Every performance number today is measured on test data.
Standardise: \(z = (x - \bar x)/s\): mean 0, spread 1
Needed for gradient descent and for KNN.
KNN: \(K\)-nearest neighbours: predict the most common class of the \(K\) closest training points
From Lecture 1; it returns in the comparison of slide 31.

title: Opening
content:
Opening# Today# Part 1: Resampling: the validation set; cross-validation; the bootstrap. Part 2: Regularisation: too many inputs; ridge regression; the lasso; choosing \(\lambda\) by cross-validation
Reading: ISLP Chapter 5 (5.1–5.2) and Chapter 6 (6.1–6.2). ESL Sections 7.10–7.11 and 3.4
ESL 7.10 covers cross-validation (including the “wrong way” of slide 10), ESL 7.11 the bootstrap, ESL 3.4 ridge and lasso.
Notebook: lecture04_resampling_regularisation.ipynb on Google Classroom
From last week: your first models# Each group fitted a first linear or logistic regression
The question for today: how well will your model do on new data?
This is what matters for a real application: a fault detector installed in a factory meets machines it never saw.
Lecture 1: the training error is too optimistic. Lecture 3: we used a separate test set. But often we have only one dataset
In Lectures 1–3 the data were simulated, so we could generate thousands of test points. A group project has one dataset, often small.
Group check (10 minutes): your model and its training error; how many rows you have; could you spare some rows for testing?
Try it: Note which groups have fewer than about 100 rows; for them cross-validation is essential.
Words from earlier lectures that we use today# Word Meaning MSE mean squared error: \(\mathrm{MSE} = \frac1n\sum_i (y_i - \hat y_i)^2\), the average squared prediction error training error the error on the data used to fit the model test error the error on new data that the model has never seen. This is what we care about overfitting the model follows the noise: small training error, large test error bias, variance bias: error from a model too simple; variance: how much the fit changes with a different sample of data hyperparameter a setting we choose rather than fit, e.g. the polynomial degree or the step size \(\alpha\) standardise \(z = (x - \bar x)/s\): every input gets mean 0 and spread 1 SE standard error: the “\(\pm\)” of an estimate This lecture leans on words from Lectures 1–3. Students who missed a class should not meet them again without a definition. Go through the table quickly, with one example each.
MSE: mean squared error, \(\mathrm{MSE} = \frac1n\sum_i (y_i - \hat y_i)^2\), the average squared prediction error
It has the units of \(y\) squared: for the thermistor, \(^\circ\)C\(^2\). Its square root is easier to picture: an MSE of 0.25 \(^\circ\)C\(^2\) is a typical error of 0.5 \(^\circ\)C.
Training error: the error on the data used to fit the model. Test error: the error on new data that the model has never seen. This is what we care about
The whole of Part 1 is about estimating the test error when we have no new data.
Overfitting: the model follows the noise: small training error, large test error
The high-degree polynomial of Lecture 1 is the standard picture.
Bias, variance: bias: error from a model too simple; variance: how much the fit changes with a different sample of data
The bias–variance trade-off of Lecture 1. Regularisation (Part 2) deliberately adds a little bias to remove a lot of variance.
Hyperparameter: a setting we choose rather than fit, e.g. the polynomial degree or the step size \(\alpha\)
Today's hyperparameters: the degree \(d\), the number of folds \(k\) and the penalty strength \(\lambda\).
Standardise: \(z = (x - \bar x)/s\): every input gets mean 0 and spread 1. SE: standard error, the “\(\pm\)” of an estimate
Standardising returns in ridge and lasso; the SE returns in the bootstrap.

content:
Opening# Today# Part 1: polynomials and step functions; splines; generalised additive models. Part 2: decision trees and pruning; bagging and random forests; boosting
Reading: ISLP Chapter 7 (7.1–7.4, 7.7) and Chapter 8 (8.1–8.2). ESL Chapters 5, 9.2, 10 and 15
ESL 5 covers splines, 9.2 trees, 10 boosting and 15 random forests, all in more mathematical depth.
Notebook: lecture05_nonlinear_trees.ipynb on Google Classroom
From last week: your cross-validation errors# Every model so far was linear in its inputs (plus products and powers we chose by hand). Today: models that find the shape themselves
In Lecture 2 we had to decide to add \(G \times T\) or take \(\ln V\). Splines and trees discover curves and interactions from the data.
Group check (10 minutes): your 10-fold CV error; compared with guessing the average (or the most common class); did the lasso drop any inputs?
Comparing with the trivial predictor tells each group whether its model has learned anything.
Try it: Ask one group to explain how they kept every step inside the folds (Lecture 4, slide 10).
Words from earlier lectures that we use today# Word Meaning residual measured minus predicted: \(y_i - \hat y_i\) overfitting the model follows the noise: small training error, large test error variance (of a model) how much the fit changes with a different sample of data hyperparameter a setting we choose rather than fit (degree, \(k\), \(\lambda\)) 10-fold CV error the test error estimated by cross-validation (Lecture 4) bootstrap sample \(n\) rows drawn with replacement from the data (Lecture 4) penalty \(\lambda\) a term added to the RSS to keep a model simple; larger \(\lambda\), simpler model (ridge, Lecture 4) test error, AUC fraction of test cases misclassified; area under the ROC curve, 1 = perfect, 0.5 = guessing (Lecture 3) noise variance the error no model can remove: the best possible MSE Today's methods are new, but they are judged and tuned with the tools of Lectures 1–4. Go through the table quickly, with one example each.
Residual: measured minus predicted, \(y_i - \hat y_i\)
Boosting fits each new tree to the residuals of the trees so far.
Overfitting: the model follows the noise. Variance (of a model): how much the fit changes with a different sample of data
A single deep tree has very high variance; bagging and random forests exist to reduce it.
Hyperparameter: a setting we choose rather than fit (degree, \(k\), \(\lambda\))
Today's hyperparameters: the number of knots, the pruning penalty, the number of trees, \(m\), the learning rate and the tree depth.
10-fold CV error: the test error estimated by cross-validation (Lecture 4). Bootstrap sample: \(n\) rows drawn with replacement from the data (Lecture 4)
Bagging is built directly on the bootstrap.
Penalty \(\lambda\): a term added to the RSS to keep a model simple; larger \(\lambda\), simpler model (ridge, Lecture 4)
The smoothing spline uses the same idea with a curvature penalty.
Test error, AUC: fraction of test cases misclassified; area under the ROC curve, 1 = perfect, 0.5 = guessing (Lecture 3)
Noise variance: the error no model can remove: the best possible MSE
For the building it is 16 kW\(^2\); every CV error today should be compared with it.
