Opening# Today# Your random forests; 2. separating classes with a hyperplane; 3. the maximal margin classifier; 4. the support vector classifier and the cost \(C\); 5. kernels: curved boundaries; 6. SVMs and logistic regression The three steps of ISLP Chapter 9: maximal margin (separable data), support vector classifier (overlapping data), support vector machine (curved boundaries).
Reading: ISLP Chapter 9 (9.1–9.5). ESL Sections 12.1–12.3
Notebook: lecture06_svm.ipynb on Google Classroom
From last week: your random forests# Trees cut the input space into boxes. Today: a method that looks for the widest gap between the classes, and can bend that gap into curves
Group check (10 minutes): random forest CV error against your baseline; your top three inputs by importance; do they make physical sense?
Try it: If a group's top input makes no physical sense, ask whether it could be leaking the answer (for example, a sample ID that is sorted by class).
Words from earlier lectures that we use today# Word Meaning decision boundary the input values where the predicted class changes (Lecture 3) loss how wrong the model is on one data point (Lectures 2–3) log loss the loss of logistic regression (cross-entropy, Lecture 3) feature another word for an input standardise \(z = (x - \bar x)/s\): every input gets mean 0 and spread 1 bias, variance bias: error from a model too simple; variance: how much the fit changes with new data hyperparameter a setting we choose rather than fit; tuned by cross-validation (Lecture 4) \(\lambda\) penalty strength in ridge and lasso (Lecture 4) SVMs are described in the language of the earlier lectures. Go through the table quickly.
Decision boundary: the input values where the predicted class changes (Lecture 3)
Today's whole topic: where to put the boundary, and how to bend it.
Loss: how wrong the model is on one data point (Lectures 2–3). Log loss: the loss of logistic regression (cross-entropy, Lecture 3)
Slide 19 compares the SVM's loss with the log loss.
Feature: another word for an input
Needed for “feature space” (slide 14).
Standardise: \(z = (x - \bar x)/s\), every input gets mean 0 and spread 1
Essential for SVMs, which measure distances.
Bias, variance: bias: error from a model too simple; variance: how much the fit changes with new data
The cost \(C\) moves along this trade-off.
Hyperparameter: a setting we choose rather than fit; tuned by cross-validation (Lecture 4). \(\lambda\): penalty strength in ridge and lasso (Lecture 4)
Today's hyperparameters, \(C\) and \(\gamma\), are tuned the same way; \(C\) plays a role like \(1/\lambda\).

title: Opening
content:
Opening# Today# Your SVMs; a network with one hidden layer; many layers and backpropagation; overfitting and regularisation; convolutional networks; recurrent networks; when to use deep learning
Reading: ISLP Chapter 10 (10.1–10.7). ESL Chapter 11
Notebook: lecture07_neural_networks.ipynb on Google Classroom. Uses PyTorch
PyTorch is the most widely used deep-learning library. It is installed in Colab.
From last week: your SVMs# SVMs bend the boundary with a kernel we choose. Today: networks that learn their own features from the raw inputs — pixels, samples of a signal
With SVMs, splines and trees, a person chooses the inputs. Networks can start from raw measurements and build useful features in their hidden layers.
Group check (10 minutes): your comparison table so far. Which model leads?
Words from earlier lectures that we use today# Word Meaning linear model \(\beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 + \dots + \beta_pX_p\): a weighted sum of the inputs (Lecture 2) sigmoid; softmax squeezes a number into a probability; turns \(K\) numbers into \(K\) probabilities (Lecture 3) loss, cost error on one point; average loss over the data. Squared error or cross-entropy (Lectures 2–3) gradient descent reduce the cost step by step against the slope, with step size \(\alpha\) (Lecture 2) chain rule the derivative of \(f(g(x))\) is \(f'(g(x))\,g'(x)\) (calculus) overfitting small training error, large test error (Lecture 1) validation set data held back to choose settings; the test set is kept for the end (Lecture 4) ridge penalty \(\lambda\sum\beta_j^2\) added to the cost to keep coefficients small (Lecture 4) A neural network is assembled from pieces students have already met. Naming them first makes the network look less like magic. Go through the table quickly.
Linear model: \(\beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 + \dots + \beta_pX_p\), a weighted sum of the inputs (Lecture 2)
Every hidden unit starts with one.
Sigmoid; softmax: squeezes a number into a probability; turns \(K\) numbers into \(K\) probabilities (Lecture 3)
Used as activation and as output layers.
Loss, cost: error on one point; average loss over the data. Squared error or cross-entropy (Lectures 2–3)
Networks are trained with exactly these costs.
Gradient descent: reduce the cost step by step against the slope, with step size \(\alpha\) (Lecture 2)
Chain rule: the derivative of \(f(g(x))\) is \(f'(g(x))\,g'(x)\) (calculus)
Backpropagation is nothing more than this rule applied layer by layer. A quick example at the board: the derivative of \((3x + 1)^2\) is \(2(3x + 1) \times 3\).
Overfitting: small training error, large test error (Lecture 1). Validation set: data held back to choose settings; the test set is kept for the end (Lecture 4)
Both are central today: networks overfit easily, and early stopping needs a validation set.
Ridge penalty: \(\lambda\sum\beta_j^2\) added to the cost to keep coefficients small (Lecture 4)
Returns as weight decay.

title: Opening
content:
Opening# Today# Part 1: principal components analysis: finding the main directions in data; how many components?; monitoring with PCA. Part 2: clustering: \(k\)-means; hierarchical clustering. Part 3: course wrap-up
Reading: ISLP Chapter 12 (12.1, 12.2, 12.4). ESL Sections 14.3 and 14.5
ESL 14.3 covers clustering, 14.5 principal components.
Notebook: lecture08_unsupervised.ipynb on Google Classroom
Learning without an output# Lectures 2–7: every example had an output \(Y\) to predict (supervised). Unsupervised: only inputs \(X_1, \dots, X_p\). No right answer to check against
This makes unsupervised learning harder to judge: there is no test error. Its results must be checked against knowledge of the problem.
Goals: summarise many variables with a few (PCA); find groups of similar objects (clustering)
Group check (10 minutes): did a neural network help on your data? Your best model so far, and its CV error
Words from earlier lectures that we use today# Word Meaning variance the spread of a variable: the average squared distance from its mean correlated two variables that tend to rise and fall together (\(r\) near \(\pm1\)); uncorrelated: \(r = 0\) standardise \(z = (x - \bar x)/s\): every variable gets mean 0 and variance 1 distance between two readings: \(\sqrt{\sum_j (x_j - x'_j)^2}\), as in KNN (Lecture 1) AUC area under the ROC curve: 1 = perfect, 0.5 = guessing (Lecture 3) false alarm a normal case flagged as a fault (false positive, Lecture 3) supervised every training example has a known output \(Y\) PCA is built on variance and correlation, and clustering on distance. Make sure these words are solid before the formulas.
Variance: the spread of a variable, the average squared distance from its mean
PCA looks for the combination of sensors with the most variance.
Correlated: two variables that tend to rise and fall together (\(r\) near \(\pm1\)); uncorrelated: \(r = 0\)
Correlated sensors are what PCA compresses: if flow and current always move together, one number describes both.
Standardise: \(z = (x - \bar x)/s\), every variable gets mean 0 and variance 1
After standardising, the total variance of 8 sensors is 8.
Distance between two readings: \(\sqrt{\sum_j (x_j - x'_j)^2}\), as in KNN (Lecture 1)
\(k\)-means and hierarchical clustering both measure similarity this way.
AUC: area under the ROC curve, 1 = perfect, 0.5 = guessing (Lecture 3). False alarm: a normal case flagged as a fault (false positive, Lecture 3)
Used to judge the PCA monitor.
Supervised: every training example has a known output \(Y\)
Today's methods have none: that is what “unsupervised” means (next slide).

title: Beyond straight lines
content:
Beyond straight lines# Example 1: a building's electricity demand# A smart electricity meter records the demand every few minutes. Photo: RobbieIanMorrison, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0 A smart meter records the power drawn by an office building. Low at night. A morning peak (about 9 am). A larger evening peak (about 7:30 pm)
A load profile like this is what an energy manager or a utility wants to predict, for example to size a solar system or plan tariffs. Energy monitoring was a survey topic.
Data: 120 readings at random times. Goal: predict demand from the hour
The relation is clearly not a straight line: it rises and falls twice.
Polynomials and step functions# Step functions jump at the bin edges; splines join smooth pieces at the knots. straight line 125.6 polynomial, degree 4 112.2 6 steps (4 h each) 80.7 Polynomial: add \(x^2, x^3, \dots, x^d\) (Lecture 2). One formula for the whole day. Low degree: too stiff for two peaks. High degree: wild near the ends
A polynomial is global: changing the fit at 9 am changes it everywhere. A degree-4 polynomial has too few turning points to follow a night–peak–dip–peak–night shape. High degrees can follow it but swing wildly near 0 and 24 h, where data are few (ISLP Figure 7.1).
Step function: cut the day into bins; predict the average in each bin. Simple, but jumps at the bin edges
With 6 bins of 4 hours, each bin predicts its average demand. A peak that lies across two bins is smeared out.
10-fold CV error (kW\(^2\)): straight line 125.6; polynomial, degree 4: 112.2; 6 steps (4 h each): 80.7. Noise variance: 16
All three are far above the noise variance of 16, the best possible.
Symbols
\(d\) Polynomial degree. kW\(^2\) Units of squared error in demand. Example: a step-function fit# Electricity demand (kW) was read at these hours:
hour 1 2 3 5 6 7 8 10 11 13 14 15 17 18 19 21 22 23 kW 18 16 17 30 44 52 49 33 28 24 26 31 45 58 61 40 30 22 Fit a step function with six 4-hour bins (0–4, 4–8, …, 20–24). What does it predict at 6:30 pm (hour 18.5) and at 9 am (hour 9)?
Solution triple-click to reveal A step function predicts the average of the readings in each bin:
bin 0–4 4–8 8–12 12–16 16–20 20–24 prediction (kW) 17.0 42.0 36.7 27.0 54.7 30.7 Hour 18.5 is in the 16–20 bin: 54.7 kW. Hour 9 is in the 8–12 bin: 36.7 kW, although the morning peak (about 50 kW at 7–8 h) is only an hour earlier: the bin edge at 8 h cuts the peak in two. This is the weakness that splines fix.
Regression splines# Choose knots: points that cut the range into pieces. 2. Fit a cubic polynomial in each piece. 3. Force the pieces to join smoothly: same value, slope and curvature at each knot A cubic spline with \(K\) interior knots has \(K + 4\) coefficients (ISLP 7.4). The joining conditions make the curve look like one smooth curve.
Still linear in the coefficients: fitted by least squares. In Python: SplineTransformer (scikit-learn)
The spline is written as a sum of fixed basis functions (B-splines) times coefficients, so the Lecture 2 machinery applies.
SplineTransformer turns the hour into B-spline columns; LinearRegression then fits them. n_knots counts all knots, evenly spaced over the data, including the two ends.
Why it works: each piece only has to follow its own part of the day. No wild swings: a change in one place stays local
Beyond the slide: natural splines A natural spline is also forced to be a straight line beyond the outer knots, which calms the ends (ISLP 7.4.4).
Four fits of the same data# Plot: line, degree 4, steps, spline (9 knots), truth
The dashed curve is the true demand (at 24 \(^\circ\)C outdoors).
The straight line and the degree-4 polynomial miss both peaks. The steps are too coarse. The spline follows both peaks
Spline, 9 knots: CV error 30.3 kW\(^2\)
Four times smaller than the straight line. The rest (30 versus 16) is mostly the effect of outdoor temperature, which this model ignores (slide 11).
Choosing the form of the curve is part of the model. xkcd #2048 “Curve-Fitting” by Randall Munroe, CC BY-NC 2.5. Hover for the alt text. How many knots? Ask cross-validation# knots 10-fold CV error 4 51.5 5 72.3 6 29.9 9 30.3 12 29.1 25 33.7 Table: 4 knots 51.5; 5: 72.3; 6: 29.9; 9: 30.3; 12: 29.1; 25: 33.7
Too few knots: cannot follow the peaks. Anything from 6 to 15 knots is about equally good. Too many knots: starts to fit the noise
With few knots the result also depends on where the evenly spaced knots happen to fall relative to the peaks; that is why 5 knots does worse than 4. From 6 knots on, the pieces are short enough to follow both peaks.
The number of knots plays the role of the polynomial degree in Lecture 4
A flexibility setting, chosen by cross-validation.
Two relatives# Smoothing spline: a knot at every data point, with a penalty on curvature: \(\mathrm{RSS} + \lambda\int g''(t)^2\,dt\). Like ridge (Lecture 4): \(\lambda\) controls how wiggly the curve may be
\(g''(t)\) is the second derivative (curvature) of the fitted curve \(g\). The integral adds up its square over the whole range. \(\lambda = 0\) lets the curve pass through every point; \(\lambda \to \infty\) forces a straight line (ISLP 7.5).
Local regression: to predict at \(x_0\), fit a straight line to the nearby points only, weighted by distance. Slide the window along \(x\). The window width controls the flexibility
Also called LOESS (ISLP 7.6). The fraction of points in the window, the span, is chosen by CV.
Students who have not met integrals recently can read \(\int\) as “add up over the whole range”.
Symbols
\(g(t)\) The fitted curve. \(g''(t)\) Its second derivative (curvature). \(\lambda\) Smoothing parameter. \(x_0\) The point where we predict. Generalised additive models (GAMs)# Several inputs, each with its own shape, added together: \(Y = \beta_0 + f_1(X_1) + f_2(X_2) + \dots + \varepsilon\)
A GAM replaces each \(\beta_jX_j\) of linear regression by a flexible function \(f_j(X_j)\) (ISLP 7.7).
Each \(f_j\) can be a spline, a straight line, or a step function, and can be plotted and interpreted on its own
The price: GAMs miss interactions unless we add them (for example, if air conditioning only runs during office hours).
Building: demand \(= f_1(\text{hour}) + \beta\,(\text{outdoor temperature})\). \(\beta\): a single slope; temperature enters as a straight line
A spline for the daily pattern, a straight line for temperature.
10-fold CV error: hour only (spline) 30.3; hour + temperature 18.8 (noise: 16). \(\hat\beta = 0.82\) kW per \(^\circ\)C (air conditioning)
Adding temperature removes most of the remaining error; the GAM is close to the best possible. The temperature coefficient (true 0.8) has a physical meaning: each extra degree outside costs 0.8 kW of cooling.
Symbols
\(f_j\) Shape function for input \(j\).

title: Logistic regression
content:
Logistic regression# Classification problems# An electric motor. Is it healthy or developing a fault? A classification question. Photo: Rama, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 fr From your survey: is a machine healthy or faulty? Is a milk sample pure or adulterated? Is a patient at high risk of asthma? Is a sensor reading normal or an anomaly? Which fault: imbalance, misalignment or bearing wear?
All five come from the problems the students named in the survey. The first four have two classes; the last has three.
Two steps: 1. Estimate the probability of each class. 2. Turn the probability into a decision
Keeping these two steps apart is the key idea of the lecture. The model gives probabilities (slides 8–15); the decision needs a threshold, which depends on the costs of mistakes (slides 16 and 23).
The last example has three classes (end of today)
Slide 32 deals with it.
Example 1: vibration and motor faults# A straight line fitted to 0/1 data predicts impossible probabilities; the logistic curve stays between 0 and 1. A motor with a worn bearing or loose mounting vibrates more
Vibration monitoring is the standard tool of predictive maintenance: a sensor (an accelerometer) on the motor housing measures how strongly it shakes. Severity is usually reported as the RMS (root-mean-square) vibration velocity in mm/s, the quantity used in the ISO vibration-severity standards.
Low vibration: almost always healthy. High vibration: almost always faulty
Between the two there is a grey zone where both happen.
Data: 200 motors. \(X\) = vibration \(v\) (RMS velocity, mm/s); \(Y\) = 1 if faulty, 0 if healthy
114 of the 200 motors are faulty.
Plot: each mark is one motor: top row faulty, bottom row healthy
Below about 3 mm/s all motors are healthy; above about 5 mm/s nearly all are faulty; in between, both.
Symbols
\(v\) RMS vibration velocity (mm/s). RMS Root mean square: \(\sqrt{\text{mean of the squared signal}}\), a measure of the size of an oscillating signal. Why not use linear regression?# Fit a straight line to the 0s and 1s: \(\hat y = -0.15 + 0.144\,v\)
We could treat 0 and 1 as numbers and fit a least-squares line (Lecture 2).
At 0 mm/s it predicts \(-0.15\). At 10 mm/s it predicts 1.29. A probability must stay between 0 and 1
\(-0.15 + 0.144 \times 0 = -0.15\) and \(-0.15 + 0.144 \times 10 = 1.29\). Neither is a possible probability.
We need a curve that stays between 0 and 1
Also, a straight line rises at the same rate everywhere, while the real probability is flat near 0, rises steeply in the grey zone, and is flat again near 1.
Plot: red, the straight-line fit; shaded, impossible values
Worked numbers
Notebook: intercept \(-0.146\), slope \(0.1438\). At \(v = 10\): \(-0.146 + 1.438 = 1.29\).
The logistic (sigmoid) function# Logistic regression in one picture: a straight-line score, squeezed by the sigmoid into a probability, then a threshold. \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\)
The logistic function, also called the sigmoid (“S-shaped”).
Any number \(z\) goes in. The output is always between 0 and 1
\(e^{-z}\) is always positive, so the denominator is always above 1 and the fraction is between 0 and 1.
\(z = 0\) gives \(\sigma = 0.5\)
\(1/(1 + e^0) = 1/2\).
Large positive \(z\): close to 1. Large negative \(z\): close to 0
\(\sigma(4) = 1/(1 + e^{-4}) = 1/1.018 = 0.982\); \(\sigma(-4) = 1/(1 + 54.6) = 0.018\).
The same Greek letter now names a function. Point this out explicitly: it is a common source of confusion.
Plot: an S-shaped curve (“sigmoid” means S-shaped)
Symbols
\(\sigma(z)\) Logistic (sigmoid) function. \(e\) Euler's number, 2.718… Try it. Move \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) until the curve follows the 0/1 data, then press Maximum likelihood. The 50% point is where the classifier switches. The logistic regression model# Put the straight line inside the sigmoid: \(p(X) = \sigma(\beta_0 + \beta_1X) = 1/(1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1X)})\)
The linear part is the same as in Lecture 2; the sigmoid squeezes it into \((0, 1)\).
The line can be any number. The sigmoid turns it into a probability. \(\beta_1 > 0\): \(p\) rises with \(X\)
If \(\beta_1 < 0\), \(p\) falls with \(X\).
\(\beta_1\) large: a sharp step. \(\beta_1\) small: a gentle slope
The steepness of the S is set by \(\beta_1\); its position by where the line crosses zero, \(X = -\beta_0/\beta_1\).
Plot: blue (\(\beta_1 = 2.5\)) crosses 0.5 at \(X = 4\); green (\(\beta_1 = 0.8\)) at \(X = 5\). \(p = 0.5\) where the line is zero: \(X = -\beta_0/\beta_1\)
Blue: \(\beta_0 = -10\), so \(X = 10/2.5 = 4\). Green: \(\beta_0 = -4\), so \(X = 4/0.8 = 5\).
Symbols
\(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\) Intercept and slope of the line inside the sigmoid. Odds and log-odds# Odds = probability of yes / probability of no: odds \(= p/(1 - p)\). \(p = 0.5\): odds 1. \(p = 0.8\): odds 4
Odds are common in everyday language (“four to one”). \(0.8/0.2 = 4\).
For logistic regression, the log-odds is a straight line: \(\ln[p/(1 - p)] = \beta_0 + \beta_1X\)
Solving \(p = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\) for \(z\) gives \(z = \ln[p/(1 - p)]\). So logistic regression is linear regression for the log-odds.
Reading \(\beta_1\): increase \(X\) by 1: the log-odds increase by \(\beta_1\). So the odds are multiplied by \(e^{\beta_1}\)
Adding \(\beta_1\) to a logarithm multiplies the quantity by \(e^{\beta_1}\). Note: it is the odds, not the probability, that change by a fixed factor.
Symbols
odds \(p/(1 - p)\), between 0 and \(\infty\). \(\ln\) Natural logarithm. Beyond the slide: from \(p\) to the log-odds \(p = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\) gives \(1 - p = e^{-z}/(1 + e^{-z})\), so \(p/(1 - p) = e^{z}\) and \(\ln[p/(1 - p)] = z\).
Example: probability, odds and log-odds# A fitted model for motor faults is \(\log\frac{p}{1-p} = -6 + 1.5\,x\), with \(x\) the vibration level (mm/s). (a) Find the probability of a fault at \(x = 5\). (b) At which vibration is the probability 50%? (c) By what factor do the odds grow for each extra 1 mm/s?
Solution triple-click to reveal (a) \(z = -6 + 1.5 \times 5 = 1.5\), so \(p = 1/(1 + e^{-1.5}) = 0.818\). The odds are \(e^{1.5} = 4.48\).
(b) \(p = 0.5\) when \(z = 0\): \(x = 6/1.5 = 4\) mm/s.
(c) The log-odds rise by 1.5 per mm/s, so the odds are multiplied by \(e^{1.5} = 4.48\).
What is a likelihood?# \(q\) 0.5 0.7 0.9 \(L(q)\) 0.0010 0.0022 0.0005 Students will need the idea of likelihood on the next slide. Introduce it first with a coin, where the answer is obvious, so the idea is clear before it is applied to motors.
Likelihood \(L\): the probability of getting the data we actually observed, if the model's parameters had a given value
The data are fixed (they have been measured); the parameter is what we vary. For each possible parameter value, the likelihood says how probable our actual data would have been.
Maximum likelihood: choose the parameters that make the observed data most probable
The principle behind most fitting methods in the course.
Example: a coin. 10 tosses give 7 heads and 3 tails. \(L(q) = q^7(1 - q)^3\). \(q = 0.5\): 0.0010; \(q = 0.7\): 0.0022; \(q = 0.9\): 0.0005. Best: \(\hat q = 0.7\) = 7 heads out of 10
Each head has probability \(q\) and each tail \(1 - q\); the tosses are independent, so the probabilities multiply. The likelihood is largest at \(q = 0.7\), which is the obvious answer, the fraction of heads.
Worked numbers
\(0.5^7 \times 0.5^3 = 0.5^{10} = 0.000977\). \(0.7^7 \times 0.3^3 = 0.0824 \times 0.027 = 0.00222\). \(0.9^7 \times 0.1^3 = 0.478 \times 0.001 = 0.00048\).
Beyond the slide: why \(\hat q = 7/10\) \(\ln L = 7\ln q + 3\ln(1 - q)\). Its derivative \(7/q - 3/(1 - q)\) is zero when \(7(1 - q) = 3q\), so \(q = 0.7\).
How do we fit it? Maximum likelihood# For each motor, the model gives a probability of what we saw: faulty (\(y_i = 1\)): probability \(p_i\); healthy (\(y_i = 0\)): probability \(1 - p_i\)
For given coefficients, the model assigns each motor a probability of being faulty, \(p_i = \sigma(\beta_0 + \beta_1v_i)\). The probability of what actually happened is \(p_i\) if the motor was faulty and \(1 - p_i\) if healthy.
Multiply over all motors: \(L(\bb) = \prod_{y_i = 1} p_i \times \prod_{y_i = 0}(1 - p_i)\)
The motors are independent, so the probability of the whole dataset is the product. \(L\) is called the likelihood.
Maximum likelihood: choose the \(\beta\)'s that make the data we observed most probable, as with the coin
Good coefficients give high \(p_i\) to faulty motors and low \(p_i\) to healthy ones, so \(L\) is large. The coin had one parameter \(q\); the motors have two, \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\), and each motor has its own probability \(p_i\).
Linear regression minimised the RSS; least squares is also maximum likelihood when the noise is Gaussian (ESL 2.6.3).
Symbols
\(p_i\) Model's probability that motor \(i\) is faulty. \(\prod\) Product (multiply all terms). \(L(\bb)\) Likelihood of the coefficients \(\bb\). Loss and cost for classification: cross-entropy# Loss for one motor: \(\ell_i = -\ln p_i\) if faulty (\(y_i = 1\)); \(-\ln(1 - p_i)\) if healthy (\(y_i = 0\))
The same loss/cost language as Lecture 2. The loss of one motor is minus the log of the probability the model gave to what really happened.
Cost = average loss \(= -\frac1n\ln L\): \(J(\bb) = -\frac1n\sum_i[y_i\ln p_i + (1 - y_i)\ln(1 - p_i)]\)
The logarithm turns the product \(L\) into a sum (easier to compute, and it avoids numbers too small for the computer). The minus sign turns maximising into minimising, and \(\frac1n\) makes it an average.
Since \(y_i\) is 0 or 1, only one of the two terms is non-zero for each motor
When \(y_i = 1\) the second term has the factor \(1 - y_i = 0\), and vice versa. The one formula covers both cases of the loss.
Loss of one faulty motor: \(p_i = 0.99\) (confident, right): 0.01; \(p_i = 0.5\) (unsure): \(\ln 2 = 0.69\); \(p_i = 0.01\) (confident, wrong): 4.6
\(-\ln 0.99 = 0.01\), \(-\ln 0.5 = 0.69\), \(-\ln 0.01 = 4.6\). Confident mistakes are punished heavily.
Minimising the cost = maximising the likelihood. The cost is called the cross-entropy or log loss
The name comes from information theory. The same cost trains neural-network classifiers (Lecture 7).
Symbols
\(\ell_i\) Loss of motor \(i\). \(J(\bb)\) Cost: average cross-entropy. Example: the cost of a confident mistake# For one machine the model gives \(p = 0.9\) for “faulty”. Compute the cross-entropy loss \(-[y\ln p + (1-y)\ln(1-p)]\) if the machine really is faulty (\(y = 1\)) and if it is healthy (\(y = 0\)).
Solution triple-click to reveal \(y = 1\): loss \(= -\ln 0.9 = 0.105\). Small: the model was confident and right.
\(y = 0\): loss \(= -\ln(1 - 0.9) = -\ln 0.1 = 2.303\). About 22 times larger: a confident wrong answer is punished hard.
Gradient descent for logistic regression# There is no formula for the best \(\bb\). We walk downhill: \(\bb \leftarrow \bb + \frac{\alpha}{n}\bX\T(\by - \bp)\)
Setting the derivatives of \(J\) to zero gives equations that cannot be solved by algebra, so we use gradient descent (Lecture 2). The gradient of the cross-entropy is \(-\frac1n\bX\T(\by - \bp)\).
Compare with linear regression (Lecture 2): \(\bb \leftarrow \bb + \frac{\alpha}{n}\bX\T(\by - \bX\bb)\)
The same rule! Step \(\propto\) (measured \(-\) predicted) \(\times\) input. Only the prediction changes: a probability instead of a straight line
This is not a coincidence; both come from maximum likelihood.
Motors: the cost falls from 0.693 to 0.140. LogisticRegression in scikit-learn gives the same answer
At the start all coefficients are zero, so every \(p_i = 0.5\) and the cost is \(\ln 2 = 0.693\). After 3000 steps (standardised input, \(\alpha = 1\)) it is 0.140. scikit-learn uses a faster method (Newton-type), with the same result.
Symbols
\(\bp\) Column of predicted probabilities. \(\alpha\) Step size. Beyond the slide: no regularisation in scikit-learn By default scikit-learn's LogisticRegression adds a penalty on large coefficients (regularisation, Lecture 4). The notebook uses C=np.inf to switch it off, so that the result is pure maximum likelihood, as in ISLP.
Motors: the result# Plot: blue, fitted curve; red, fraction faulty in each 1-mm/s bin
The red dots are simple counts: for example, of the motors between 4 and 5 mm/s, 62% were faulty. The fitted S-curve passes through them.
\(\hat p(v) = \sigma(-10.1 + 2.39\,v)\)
The maximum-likelihood fit.
50% point: \(-10.1 + 2.39\,v = 0\), so \(v = 4.2\) mm/s
Where the line inside the sigmoid is zero. The true value in the simulation is 4.0 mm/s.
Each extra mm/s multiplies the odds of a fault by \(e^{2.39} = 10.9\)
Slide 10 in action.
\(\hat\beta_1 = 2.39\), SE \(= 0.45\), \(z = 2.39/0.45 = 5.3\): a real effect
As in Lecture 2, each coefficient has a standard error. The ratio is called \(z\) here (ISLP Table 4.1); \(\vert z\vert > 2\) means the effect is real.
In maintenance words: below 2 mm/s, under 1% fault chance. Above 6 mm/s, over 98%
Symbols
\(\hat p(v)\) Estimated probability of a fault at vibration \(v\). \(z\) Estimate divided by its standard error. Worked numbers
50% point: \(10.10/2.386 = 4.24\) mm/s. Odds factor: \(e^{2.386} = 10.9\). \(z = 2.386/0.452 = 5.3\).
\(\hat p(2) = \sigma(-10.10 + 4.77) = \sigma(-5.33) = 0.005\); \(\hat p(6) = \sigma(-10.10 + 14.32) = \sigma(4.22) = 0.985\).
Beyond the slide: where the SE comes from \(\mathrm{SE}^2\) is the diagonal of \((\bX\T\mathbf W\bX)^{-1}\), with \(\mathbf W\) diagonal, \(W_{ii} = p_i(1 - p_i)\) (ESL 4.4.1). The notebook computes this.
From a probability to a decision# To classify, choose a threshold, usually 0.5: predict 1 if \(\hat p \ge 0.5\)
With threshold 0.5 we predict the more probable class.
\(\hat p \ge 0.5\) is the same as \(\beta_0 + \beta_1X \ge 0\)
Because \(\sigma(z) \ge 0.5\) exactly when \(z \ge 0\).
The decision boundary is where \(\beta_0 + \beta_1X = 0\). For the motors: \(v = 4.2\) mm/s
Motors above 4.2 mm/s are called faulty.
Logistic regression gives a probability. The threshold turns it into a yes/no decision. We choose the threshold (later today)
How to choose it is slide 23.
Example 2: two sensors on each machine# A monitoring system records two inputs for each machine: vibration \(v\) (mm/s); bearing temperature \(T\) (\(^\circ\)C)
A failing bearing both vibrates and heats up through friction. Using both sensors should classify better than either alone.
Faulty machines vibrate more and run hotter, but the groups overlap
The overlap means some errors are unavoidable (the Bayes error of Lecture 1).
Data: 400 training machines (122 faulty), 2000 test machines (593 faulty)
A separate test set, as Lecture 1 taught: every performance number is measured on the 2000 machines not used in training.
Plot: training machines (simulated)
Healthy machines form a compact cloud; faulty ones are more spread out and stretched along a diagonal, because in faulty machines high vibration and high temperature go together.
Two inputs: the decision boundary is a line# \(\hat p = \sigma(-15.8 + 1.28\,v + 0.199\,T)\)
Logistic regression with two inputs.
The boundary \(\hat p = 0.5\) is where \(-15.8 + 1.28\,v + 0.199\,T = 0\)
This is a straight line: \(T = 79.6 - 6.41\,v\)
Solve for \(T\). A machine at 2 mm/s is called faulty above \(79.6 - 12.8 = 66.8~^\circ\)C; at 5 mm/s, above \(47.5~^\circ\)C. High vibration and high temperature can each push a machine over the line.
Above the line: faulty. Below the line: healthy
Worked numbers
\(15.84/0.1991 = 79.6\); \(1.276/0.1991 = 6.41\).

title: Neural networks
content:
Neural networks# A network with one hidden layer# The Mark I Perceptron (1958): the first neural network, built in hardware. Photo: John C. Hay, Albert E. Murray, Wikimedia Commons, Public domain One neuron: weight the inputs, add them, pass the result through an activation. Diagram: inputs \(X_1, \dots, X_4\); hidden layer \(A_1, \dots, A_5\); output \(f\)
Every input connects to every hidden unit, and every hidden unit to the output: a fully connected (dense) network.
Each hidden unit \(k\): \(A_k = g(w_{k0} + \sum_jw_{kj}X_j)\): a linear model
Each hidden unit computes its own linear combination of the inputs, then passes it through \(g\). The weights \(w\) are learned.
The output adds them up: \(f(X) = \beta_0 + \sum_k\beta_kA_k\)
The output is a linear model in the hidden units (ISLP equation 10.1). For classification, a sigmoid is applied to \(f\).
\(g\) is a non-linear activation function. Hidden: neither input nor output; we never observe it
Symbols
\(X_j\) Input \(j\). \(A_k\) Activation (output) of hidden unit \(k\). \(w_{k0}, w_{kj}\) Bias and weights of hidden unit \(k\). \(g\) Activation function. \(\beta_0, \beta_k\) Bias and weights of the output. Example: a forward pass by hand# A network has 2 inputs, 2 hidden ReLU units and one linear output: \(h_1 = \mathrm{ReLU}(x_1 + 2x_2)\), \(h_2 = \mathrm{ReLU}(-x_1 + 0.5x_2 + 1)\), \(\hat y = 1.5h_1 - 2h_2 + 0.5\). Compute \(\hat y\) for \(\mathbf x = (0.5, -1)\).
Solution triple-click to reveal \(h_1 = \mathrm{ReLU}(0.5 - 2) = \mathrm{ReLU}(-1.5) = 0\).
\(h_2 = \mathrm{ReLU}(-0.5 - 0.5 + 1) = \mathrm{ReLU}(0) = 0\).
\(\hat y = 1.5(0) - 2(0) + 0.5 = 0.5\). Both hidden units are switched off here, so only the output bias is left.
Activation functions# The three most common activation functions. Sigmoid: \(g(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\) (Lecture 3). ReLU: \(g(z) = \max(0, z)\), the rectified linear unit. Fast, and the usual choice today
ReLU passes positive values unchanged and sets negative ones to zero. Its gradient is 1 or 0, which keeps training fast in deep networks; the sigmoid's gradient becomes tiny for large \(\vert z\vert \).
\(z\): the number that goes in (the linear model); \(\max(0, z)\): \(z\) if positive, otherwise 0
Why non-linear? Without \(g\), a network is just one big linear model, however many layers it has
A linear function of a linear function is linear. The non-linearity lets the network bend and combine.
Try it. Change the weight and the bias, then switch between sigmoid, tanh and ReLU. The weight sets how sharp the switch is; the bias moves it. Many layers# A network with two hidden layers: every unit feeds every unit of the next layer. A deep network stacks hidden layers: each layer's outputs are the next layer's inputs. Early layers: simple features. Later layers: combinations of features
In image networks, early layers respond to edges and spots; later ones to shapes made of them.
Output layer: one unit with a sigmoid for yes/no; \(K\) units with softmax for \(K\) classes (Lecture 3); one plain unit for regression
The word “bias” now has two meanings in the course.
Counting parameters: a layer from \(a\) units to \(b\) units has \(a \times b\) weights \(+ b\) biases
6 inputs, 64, 64, 1 output: \(6 \times 64 + 64 = 448\); \(64 \times 64 + 64 = 4160\); \(64 \times 1 + 1 = 65\). Total 4673 parameters
From 2000 training machines. Compare logistic regression: 7 parameters.
Symbols
\(a\), \(b\) Units in consecutive layers. Example: counting parameters# A network for the six-sensor machines has 6 inputs, a hidden layer of 32 units, a second hidden layer of 16 units, and 1 output. How many weights and biases does it learn? Compare with logistic regression on the same inputs.
Solution triple-click to reveal Each layer has (inputs × units) weights plus one bias per unit:
6 → 32: \(6 \times 32 + 32 = 224\) 32 → 16: \(32 \times 16 + 16 = 528\) 16 → 1: \(16 \times 1 + 1 = 17\) Total 769 parameters, against 7 for logistic regression. With a few hundred machines that is a lot: regularisation and early stopping matter.
Fitting a network# Loss: squared error (regression) or cross-entropy (classification) — as in Lectures 2 and 3
Gradient descent (Lecture 2), with two additions: backpropagation: the chain rule gives every gradient, working backwards from the output; minibatches: each step uses a small random batch (e.g. 64 rows). One pass through the data is an epoch
Backpropagation is the chain rule organised efficiently: the error at the output is passed back layer by layer, giving the derivative of the loss with respect to every weight in about the cost of one forward pass (ISLP 10.7). With 2000 rows and batches of 64, one epoch is 32 steps.
Not a single bowl: the loss has many valleys. Different starting weights (seeds) give different networks
Unlike linear and logistic regression, there is no guarantee of the best answer. In practice many valleys are about equally good.
Backpropagation in words# Forward pass to compute the loss; backward pass (the chain rule) to compute every gradient. The name “backpropagation” frightens students. This slide shows it is the chain rule plus bookkeeping.
Forward pass: feed a minibatch through the network, layer by layer, to get the predictions. 2. Loss: compare the predictions with the true outputs Exactly as for any model: predict, then measure the error.
Backward pass: start at the output and go back layer by layer. The chain rule says how much each weight changed the loss: its gradient For an output weight, the gradient is (error) \(\times\) (the hidden unit's value), as in linear regression. For a weight one layer down, the chain rule multiplies by the output weight and by the slope of the activation \(g\). Each layer reuses the numbers already computed for the layer above.
Update: move every weight a small step against its gradient (gradient descent). 5. Repeat with the next minibatch Why “back”: a weight in an early layer affects the loss only through the later layers. So its gradient is built from the later layers' gradients, which are computed first
In PyTorch: loss.backward() does step 3; optimizer.step() does step 4. We use the Adam optimiser, a gradient descent that adapts the step size for each weight
Adam adapts the step size for each weight from recent gradients; it needs little tuning.
Worked numbers
One input \(x = 2\), one hidden ReLU unit with weight \(w = 0.5\), output weight \(\beta = 3\), target \(y = 1\), loss \(\frac12(y - \hat y)^2\). Forward: \(A = \max(0, 0.5 \times 2) = 1\); \(\hat y = 3 \times 1 = 3\); loss \(= \frac12(1 - 3)^2 = 2\). Backward: \(\partial\text{loss}/\partial\hat y = \hat y - y = 2\); \(\partial\text{loss}/\partial\beta = 2 \times A = 2\); \(\partial\text{loss}/\partial w = 2 \times \beta \times g'(1) \times x = 2 \times 3 \times 1 \times 2 = 12\).
Six-sensor machines again# Model parameters train test Logistic regression 7 0.146 0.149 Network, 16 hidden 129 0.086 0.099 Network, 64 + 64 4673 0.000 0.125 Network, 64 + 64, dropout 4673 0.049 0.080 Random forest (300 trees) 0.048 Table: logistic regression 7 parameters, train 0.146, test 0.149; network 16 hidden: 129, 0.086, 0.099; 64 + 64: 4673, 0.000, 0.125; 64 + 64 with dropout: 4673, 0.049, 0.080; random forest test 0.048. Best possible about 0.05
The same rules as Lecture 5, now with 2000 training machines. All networks trained for 200 epochs.
The big network memorises the training data: error 0
Including the 5% of labels that are random: a sure sign of overfitting.
Dropout (explained shortly) helps a lot
From 0.125 to 0.080.
The random forest still wins on this table of sensor readings
Its error 0.048 is at the floor. The fault rules are thresholds, which trees represent exactly; a network must build them out of smooth pieces.
Worked numbers
16 hidden units: \(6 \times 16 + 16 = 112\), plus \(16 + 1 = 17\): 129 parameters. No hidden layer: \(6 + 1 = 7\) — exactly logistic regression (notebook question 1: same test error, 0.149).
Try it. Press Train and watch a small network learn a boundary no straight line can draw. Try 1 hidden unit, then 8. Overfitting as training goes on# Stop training when the validation loss stops falling. Plot: training loss and test error against epoch, network 64 + 64, no dropout
Recorded every 10 epochs.
The training loss falls towards 0. The test error is lowest early (0.097 at epoch 10), then rises to 0.12
Training loss 0.25 at epoch 10, 0.004 at epoch 170. Test error 0.097, 0.102, 0.113, 0.120, 0.124 at epochs 10, 50, 90, 130, 170: the longer it trains, the more it fits noise.
Early stopping: keep back a validation set. Stop when its error stops improving
We used the test set in the plot only to show the effect; in practice, a validation set taken from the training data decides when to stop, and the test set is used once at the end.
Epoch: one pass through all the training data
A trained network is only as good as what it was trained on. xkcd #2173 “Trained a Neural Net” by Randall Munroe, CC BY-NC 2.5. Hover for the alt text. Regularising a network# Dropout: during training, switch off each hidden unit at random (here 30% of the time). No unit can rely on another
At prediction time all units are used (with weights scaled). Dropout acts like training many thinned networks and averaging them, similar to bagging (Lecture 5).
Weight decay: add \(\lambda\sum w^2\) to the loss: ridge regression (Lecture 4) for networks. \(w\): the weights; \(\lambda\): penalty strength
Early stopping: stop training when the validation error is lowest
Networks have many parameters, so they almost always need at least one of these

title: Principal components analysis
content:
Principal components analysis# Example: a pump station# A pumping station with five sensors that usually move together. Photo: Rhododendrites, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 A water pump is monitored by 8 sensors: flow; discharge pressure; suction pressure; motor current; motor power; bearing, motor and oil temperatures
A typical supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) record at a water utility.
Data: 500 readings of normal operation
Eight numbers per reading, but they move together. How many things are really changing?
When the pump works harder, flow, pressure, current and power all rise; when the day is hot, all temperatures rise.
The idea of PCA: find a few new variables, combinations of the 8 sensors, that capture most of the variation
Standardise first: the sensors have different units
Otherwise the sensor with the largest numbers (for example pressure in kPa) would dominate the variance.
Principal components# PCA finds the direction of largest spread, then the next one at right angles. The first principal component is the combination \(Z_1 = \phi_{11}X_1 + \dots + \phi_{p1}X_p\) with the largest variance, where \(\sum_j\phi_{j1}^2 = 1\)
Without the constraint, the variance could be made as large as we like by multiplying all \(\phi\) by a big number.
The second, \(Z_2\), has the largest variance among combinations uncorrelated with \(Z_1\); and so on
There are at most \(p\) components. Mathematically, the loading vectors are the eigenvectors of the correlation matrix of the data, and their variances are the eigenvalues (ESL 14.5.1).
Two words: loadings \(\phi_{j1}\): how much each sensor contributes. Scores \(z_{i1}\): the value of \(Z_1\) for reading \(i\)
Geometrically: the direction in which the cloud of points is most stretched
In 8 dimensions the readings form a flattened cloud; PC1 is its longest axis, PC2 the next.
Symbols
\(Z_m\) The \(m\)-th principal component. \(\phi_{jm}\) Loading of sensor \(j\) on component \(m\). \(z_{im}\) Score of reading \(i\) on component \(m\). \(p\) Number of variables (8). Try it. Turn the direction. The orange dots are the points projected onto the line; their spread is the variance along that direction. PC1 makes it as large as possible; PC2 is at right angles. How much does each component explain?# Plot: variance explained by each component and cumulative. PC1: 69.8%. PC2: 22.8%. PC3 to PC8: 1–2% each (noise)
The proportion of variance explained (PVE) of a component is its variance divided by the total variance (8, after standardising).
Scree plot: look for the elbow. Here: 2 components explain 92.6%
The name comes from the pile of rubble (scree) at the foot of a cliff: the small components after the elbow.
Worked numbers
\(69.8 + 22.8 = 92.6\%\). PC1's variance is \(0.698 \times 8 = 5.6\) standardised sensors' worth; each noise component is about \(0.012 \times 8 = 0.1\), close to the noise variance per standardised sensor.
Example: proportion of variance explained# A PCA of five standardised pump-station sensors gives the variances (eigenvalues) 3.2, 1.5, 0.8, 0.3 and 0.2. Compute the proportion of variance explained by each component and the cumulative proportion. How many components keep at least 90%?
Solution triple-click to reveal The total variance of five standardised inputs is 5.0 (one per input). Dividing:
component 1 2 3 4 5 PVE 0.53 0.25 0.13 0.05 0.03 cumulative 0.53 0.78 0.92 0.97 1.00 Three components keep 92% (two keep only 78%): three numbers per reading instead of five.
What do the components mean? The loadings# Bar chart: PC1 and PC2 loadings for the 8 sensors
PC1: flow \(+0.38\), discharge pressure \(+0.39\), suction pressure \(-0.37\), current \(+0.39\), power \(+0.39\), temperatures \(+0.23\) to \(+0.33\). PC2: the three temperatures \(+0.42\) to \(+0.59\), the hydraulic and electrical sensors \(-0.18\) to \(-0.27\), suction pressure \(+0.25\).
PC1 = “load”: flow, pressure, current and power rise together; suction pressure falls
A pump drawing more water lowers the pressure at its inlet.
PC2 = “temperature”: the three temperatures, against the hydraulic sensors
Eight sensors, but only two things really change: how hard the pump works, and how warm it is
These match the two hidden factors used to simulate the data.
The scores: each reading as two numbers# Each dot is one reading of all 8 sensors. A plot of 2 numbers instead of 8: easy to watch on a control-room screen
PCA scores can also be the inputs to a regression (principal components regression)
With many correlated inputs, regressing on a few components is an alternative to ridge and lasso (ISLP 6.3.1).
Monitoring with PCA# Learn what normal looks like; a reading far from it is an anomaly. Normal readings lie close to the plane of PC1 and PC2
92.6% of the variation is in that plane; the rest is small noise.
Reconstruction error: project a new reading onto the 2 components, rebuild the 8 sensor values, and measure how far off they are: error \(= \sum_j(z_j - \hat z_j)^2\)
\(\hat z_j\) is the value of standardised sensor \(j\) predicted from the two scores. The error is the squared distance from the reading to the plane (the \(Q\) or SPE statistic of process monitoring).
Large error: the sensors no longer agree with each other
A partial blockage: motor current up, but flow down. Each sensor alone looks normal; together they break the usual pattern
Normally current and flow rise together. A blockage makes the motor work harder for less water.
Test: 900 normal and 100 blocked readings
Symbols
\(z_j\) Standardised value of sensor \(j\). \(\hat z_j\) Its reconstruction from 2 components. Monitoring: the result# Alarm based on AUC the most extreme single sensor 0.75 PCA reconstruction error 0.99 Table: alarm based on the most extreme single sensor: AUC 0.75; PCA reconstruction error: AUC 0.99
AUC as in Lecture 3.
Alarm when the error exceeds its 99th percentile on normal data (the value only 1% of normal readings exceed): 88% of blockages caught; 1.3% false alarms
The threshold (1.66) was set on the 500 normal training readings so that 1% of them would raise an alarm; on new normal readings the rate is 1.3%.
No fault labels needed: the monitor was built from normal data only. It flags anything that does not look normal
Useful when faults are rare and varied, as in most plants.
This answers the survey problems “anomaly detection from sensor data” and “early fault detection”

title: Resampling
content:
Resampling# Example: calibrating a thermistor# An NTC thermistor: its resistance falls with temperature along a curve, not a line. Photo: Soumyapatra13, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 An NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient) is a resistor whose resistance \(R\) falls steeply as it warms
NTC means negative temperature coefficient. Thermistors are cheap, sensitive temperature sensors used in appliances, cars and instruments.
Data: 40 readings of \(R\) (k\(\Omega\)) against a reference thermometer, 0 to 100 \(^\circ\)C
The resistance falls from about 33 k\(\Omega\) at 0 \(^\circ\)C to 0.7 k\(\Omega\) at 100 \(^\circ\)C.
Model: predict \(T\) from \(x = \ln R\) with a polynomial: \(T = \beta_0 + \beta_1x + \dots + \beta_dx^d\)
Physics (the \(B\)-parameter equation) says \(1/T_K\) is linear in \(\ln R\), so \(T\) is a smooth curve in \(\ln R\). A polynomial in \(\ln R\) is still linear in the coefficients (Lecture 2).
Question: which degree \(d\)?
Too low underfits; too high fits the noise (Lecture 1). We need the test error of each degree, but have only 40 readings.
Plot: 10 k\(\Omega\) at 25 \(^\circ\)C; 0.7 k\(\Omega\) at 100 \(^\circ\)C. Log scale
Symbols
\(R\) Resistance (k\(\Omega\)). \(T\), \(T_K\) Temperature in \(^\circ\)C; in kelvin, \(T_K = T + 273.15\). \(x\) \(\ln R\), the input. \(d\) Degree of the polynomial. \(B\) Thermistor constant (3950 K here). Worked numbers
At 100 \(^\circ\)C: \(R = 10\exp[3950(1/373.15 - 1/298.15)] = 10\exp(3950 \times (-0.000674)) = 10\exp(-2.662) = 0.70\) k\(\Omega\).
The validation set approach# Two ways to keep data aside: one split, or leave out one point at a time. Split the data at random into two halves. 2. Fit on the training half. 3. Measure the MSE on the validation half The simplest idea: hold back part of the data and use it as a test set.
Plot: ten different random splits of the same 40 readings
Each curve is the validation MSE against degree for one split. All agree that degree 1 is bad (MSE about 7), but they disagree about the rest.
Two problems: the answer depends on the split: 10 splits pick degrees from 2 to 9. Only half the data are used for fitting
With 20 validation points, the estimate is noisy: the best degree in the 10 splits was 5, 3, 2, 8, 4, 3, 9, 3, 2, 3. And a model fitted on 20 points is worse than one fitted on 40, so the validation error overestimates the error of the final model.
The two words are easily confused. A validation set is used to make a choice (which degree), so it influences the final model. A test set only reports how good the final model is, and is never used to choose anything (slide 23).
Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV)# Leave out reading 1. Fit on the other \(n - 1\). 2. Predict reading 1: error \(\mathrm{MSE}_1\). 3. Repeat for every reading Each reading takes a turn as a one-point test set.
\(\mathrm{CV}_{(n)} = \frac1n\sum_i \mathrm{MSE}_i\)
The average of the \(n\) squared prediction errors. Here \(\mathrm{MSE}_i = (y_i - \hat y_{(-i)})^2\), where \(\hat y_{(-i)}\) is the prediction from the model fitted without reading \(i\).
Good: every fit uses almost all the data. No randomness: always the same answer
Bad: \(n\) fits. Slow for big data or slow models
For least squares there is a shortcut that needs only one fit (ISLP equation 5.2), but not for most other methods.
“\((-i)\)” means “with point \(i\) removed”.
Symbols
\(n\) Number of data points (40). \(\mathrm{MSE}_i\) Squared error on point \(i\) when it is left out. \(\mathrm{CV}_{(n)}\) LOOCV estimate of the test MSE. \(k\)-fold cross-validation# 5-fold cross-validation: every point is used once to measure the error. Split the data into \(k\) groups (folds). 2. Leave out fold 1; fit on the rest; compute \(\mathrm{MSE}_1\) on fold 1. 3. Repeat for every fold A compromise between the validation set (\(k = 2\), used once) and LOOCV (\(k = n\)).
\(\mathrm{CV}_{(k)} = \frac1k\sum_j \mathrm{MSE}_j\)
Usual choice: \(k = 5\) or \(k = 10\)
With \(k = 10\) and \(n = 40\), each fit uses 36 points and each fold tests 4.
Diagram: \(k = 5\). Red: left-out fold. Blue: used for fitting
Every point is left out exactly once.
Note the clash of letters: ISLP uses \(K\) for both the folds and the neighbours of KNN.
Symbols
\(k\) Number of folds. \(\mathrm{MSE}_j\) MSE on fold \(j\) when it is left out. Example: the 5-fold cross-validation estimate# A thermistor model is fitted 5 times, each time leaving out one fold. The MSEs on the left-out folds are 0.41, 0.38, 0.52, 0.45 and 0.39 °C². What is the cross-validation estimate of the test MSE, and how many model fits did it cost? How many would LOOCV cost with \(n = 60\) readings?
Solution triple-click to reveal \[ \mathrm{CV}_{(5)} = \frac{1}{5}(0.41 + 0.38 + 0.52 + 0.45 + 0.39) = 0.430\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}^2. \]It cost 5 fits. LOOCV leaves out one reading at a time: 60 fits (for least squares there is a shortcut formula, but not for most methods).
Thermistor: cross-validation picks the degree# Plot: training, LOOCV, 10-fold CV and true test MSE against degree
Because the data are simulated, we can also compute the true test error on 5000 new readings, and check how well CV estimated it.
Training MSE keeps falling
From 6.64 at degree 1 to 0.17 at degree 8: more flexibility always fits the training data better. (At degree 10 even the training MSE rises, to 0.93: \(x^{10}\) is so large that rounding errors spoil the least-squares solve.)
LOOCV and 10-fold CV both pick \(d = 3\) (MSE 0.25)
LOOCV 0.254, 10-fold 0.253.
The true test MSE, from 5000 new readings, is also lowest at \(d = 3\) (0.34)
CV chose correctly. The level differs a little (0.25 versus 0.34) because 40 points give a noisy estimate, but the shape and the minimum agree.
CV finds the right model without a separate test set
Worked numbers
Irreducible error: the reference noise is 0.5 \(^\circ\)C, variance 0.25; the 1% noise on \(R\) adds about \((0.01 \times \vert \mathrm{d}T/\mathrm{d}\ln R\vert )^2\), with \(\vert \mathrm{d}T/\mathrm{d}\ln R\vert = T_K^2/B = 323^2/3950 = 26\) K at 50 \(^\circ\)C, i.e. \((0.26)^2 = 0.07\). Total about 0.32, close to the best test MSE of 0.34.
Try it. Change K. Each row is one fit; orange is the left-out fold. The CV error curve chooses the polynomial degree. Which \(k\)? And a warning# LOOCV vs 10-fold: LOOCV: less bias (each fit uses \(n - 1\) points) but more variance (the \(n\) fits are almost identical, so their errors do not average out). 10-fold: 10 fits instead of \(n\), and usually just as good
The \(n\) LOOCV fits are almost identical, so their errors are highly correlated and their average is noisy. 10-fold CV is the standard choice (ISLP 5.1.4).
Classification: use the error rate in each fold instead of the MSE
Do every step inside the folds: if you choose inputs using all the data and then cross-validate, the CV error is far too optimistic. Every step that looks at \(Y\) — choosing inputs, scaling, tuning — must be repeated inside each fold
The classic mistake (ESL 7.10.2): with 5000 random inputs and 50 samples, pick the 100 most correlated with \(Y\), then cross-validate: CV reports near-zero error on pure noise. The left-out fold had already been used to choose the inputs. In scikit-learn a Pipeline keeps every step inside the folds.
The bootstrap# The bootstrap: resample the data with replacement, recompute the estimate many times, and look at the spread. How uncertain is a number that has no SE formula?
Lecture 2 gave SE formulas for regression coefficients. For most other quantities there is no formula.
Draw \(n\) rows with replacement from the data. 2. Compute the number again. 3. Repeat \(B = 1000\) times. 4. The spread of the \(B\) values is the SE The idea: we cannot collect 1000 new datasets, but we can imitate them by resampling the one we have.
With replacement: some rows appear twice or more, some not at all. Each bootstrap sample is a plausible “other dataset”
On average a bootstrap sample contains about 63% of the distinct rows (notebook question 4).
Example: the 50% vibration point of Lecture 3: \(v_{50} = -\hat\beta_0/\hat\beta_1\), where the fitted probability of a fault is 0.5. There is no simple SE formula
It is a ratio of two estimates, whose errors are correlated.
Symbols
\(B\) Number of bootstrap samples. \(v_{50}\) Vibration at which the fault probability is 50%. Worked numbers
Probability that a given row is never drawn in \(n\) draws: \((1 - 1/n)^n\); for \(n = 200\) this is \(0.995^{200} = 0.367 \approx e^{-1}\). So about \(0.367 \times 200 \approx 73\) motors are missing from each bootstrap sample, and 63% are present.
Example: how many readings does a bootstrap sample miss?# A bootstrap sample draws \(n\) readings with replacement from \(n\). What is the probability that one given reading is never drawn, for \(n = 10\) and for \(n = 1000\)?
Solution triple-click to reveal One draw misses it with probability \(1 - 1/n\); \(n\) independent draws all miss it with probability \((1 - 1/n)^n\).
\(n = 10\): \(0.9^{10} = 0.349\) \(n = 1000\): \(0.999^{1000} = 0.368\), close to \(e^{-1} = 0.368\). So each bootstrap sample leaves out about a third of the readings (these are the “out-of-bag” readings used in Lecture 5).
Bootstrap: the 50% vibration point# Histogram: 1000 bootstrap estimates. Dashed: the true value, 4.0
Each bar counts how many of the 1000 refits gave a 50% point in that range.
Result: estimate 4.24 mm/s; bootstrap SE 0.14 mm/s; \(v_{50} = 4.24 \pm 0.14\) mm/s
The SE is the standard deviation of the 1000 values.
95% interval (\(\pm\) about 2 SE): \([3.96, 4.51]\). The true value, 4.0, is inside
The percentile interval: the 2.5% and 97.5% points of the 1000 values. It is close to \(4.24 \pm 2 \times 0.14 = [3.96, 4.52]\).
The same recipe works for almost any number computed from data
A median, a correlation, an AUC, a time constant.
Try it. Draw bootstrap samples. The histogram of the estimates is the uncertainty, without any formula.

title: Simple linear regression
content:
Simple linear regression# What is linear regression?# An LM35 temperature sensor: its output voltage rises in a straight line with temperature. Calibrating it is a linear regression. Photo: Nevit Dilmen (talk), Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 We have inputs \(X\) and a numerical output \(Y\)
Linear regression is a supervised method for regression problems: the output is a number.
We assume \(Y\) changes in a straight line with \(X\)
With one input: each extra unit of \(X\) changes \(Y\) by the same amount, wherever we are on the line.
Real relationships are rarely exactly straight, but often close enough
Over a limited range, many relations are nearly straight. A linear model is simple, fast and easy to interpret, and often predicts well.
The coefficients \(\beta_0, \beta_1, \dots\) (“beta”) are the numbers the model learns from the data
A model has a fixed form, chosen by us, and some numbers left open. Fitting the model means finding those numbers from the data. \(\beta\) is the Greek letter beta; the small number underneath only counts the coefficients.
“Linear” means linear in the coefficients. A curve such as \(Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1X + \beta_2X^2\) still counts
The word “linear” refers to how the unknown coefficients appear, not to the shape of the graph. \(\beta_0 + \beta_1X + \beta_2X^2\) is a parabola in \(X\), but it is a sum of coefficients times known numbers (\(1\), \(X\), \(X^2\)), so the same method fits it. Slide 23 uses this.
“All models are wrong, but some are useful.” — George Box
George Box was a British statistician. No model captures reality exactly; the question is whether it is good enough for the purpose.
You already fit straight lines in the lab (Ohm's law, sensor calibration). Today we do it properly, and we find the uncertainty of the result
Students have drawn best-fit lines by eye or with a calculator. Today: the exact method (least squares), and how to say how sure we are of the slope and intercept.
Symbols
\(X\), \(Y\) Input and output. \(\beta_0, \beta_1, \beta_2\) Coefficients (unknown numbers) of the model. A straight line is a model; whether it is a good one is what this lecture is about. xkcd #1725 “Linear Regression” by Randall Munroe, CC BY-NC 2.5. Hover for the alt text. The model with one input# \(Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1X + \varepsilon\): output = intercept + slope \(\times\) input + random error
The simple linear regression model. \(\beta_0\) is the value of \(Y\) when \(X = 0\); \(\beta_1\) is the change in \(Y\) for each unit increase of \(X\); \(\varepsilon\) is everything the straight line does not capture (noise, unmeasured effects), with mean zero.
\(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\) are unknown. From data we compute estimates \(\hat\beta_0\), \(\hat\beta_1\) and predict \(\hat y = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1x\)
The true coefficients are never known exactly; we estimate them from \(n\) data points. Once estimated, a prediction for any new input \(x\) is \(\hat y\).
The Symbols box reads the equation in words. Note that \(\varepsilon\) is not a mistake in the model but the scatter of real measurements: two readings at the same temperature never give exactly the same voltage.
Calibrating a temperature sensor: an analogue sensor gives a voltage \(V\) that rises with temperature \(T\): \(V = \beta_0 + \beta_1 T\). \(\beta_1\): sensitivity (mV/\(^\circ\)C); \(\beta_0\): offset (mV). Data: 20 readings against a reference thermometer. Datasheet: 10 mV/\(^\circ\)C, no offset
Calibration is a daily task in instrumentation, and it is a linear regression. Sensors such as the LM35 give an output voltage proportional to temperature. Here the input is the true temperature from a trusted reference thermometer, and the output is the sensor voltage. The slope is the sensitivity: millivolts per degree. The intercept is the offset: the output at 0 \(^\circ\)C. The datasheet promises 10 mV/\(^\circ\)C and zero offset. Our job: measure both, with their uncertainties, and check the datasheet.
Symbols
\(\varepsilon\) Random error, mean zero. \(\hat\beta_0\), \(\hat\beta_1\) Estimates of the intercept and slope. \(\hat y\) Predicted output for input \(x\). \(V\) Sensor output voltage (mV). \(T\) Temperature from the reference thermometer (\(^\circ\)C). Least squares: what is the “best” line?# Least squares makes the total area of the squared residuals as small as possible. Residual = measured \(-\) predicted: \(e_i = y_i - \hat y_i\)
For each data point, the residual is the vertical distance from the point to the line: positive if the point is above the line, negative if below.
Residual sum of squares: \(\mathrm{RSS} = e_1^2 + e_2^2 + \dots + e_n^2\)
Square each residual (so that positive and negative ones do not cancel, and large ones count heavily) and add them up.
The best line has the smallest RSS: least squares
Of all possible straight lines, choose the one with the smallest RSS. This is the “evaluation” part of slide 3.
Plot: 20 calibration readings and the least-squares line
The readings lie very close to a straight line: the sensor is linear, and the noise (about 15 mV) is small compared with the range of the output (60 to 920 mV).
Without squaring, a line far above some points and far below others could have residuals that add to zero. Squares are always positive.
Symbols
\(e_i\) Residual of point \(i\) (units of \(y\), here mV). \(y_i\), \(\hat y_i\) Measured and predicted output of point \(i\). RSS Residual sum of squares (units of \(y\) squared, mV\(^2\)). \(n\) Number of data points (here 20). Try it. Move the intercept and the slope. The red lines are the residuals; least squares makes the sum of their squares (the RSS) as small as possible. Then press Least squares. The least-squares line# Set the derivatives of the RSS to zero and solve: \(\hat\beta_1 = \sum_i(x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y) / \sum_i(x_i - \bar x)^2\), \(\hat\beta_0 = \bar y - \hat\beta_1\bar x\)
The RSS is a function of the two unknowns \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\). At its minimum both partial derivatives are zero. Solving these two equations gives the two formulas. The second formula says the least-squares line always passes through the point of averages \((\bar x, \bar y)\).
In words: the slope is how \(x\) and \(y\) vary together, divided by how much \(x\) varies
The numerator is large and positive when points with \(x\) above average also have \(y\) above average. The denominator measures the spread of \(x\).
Your turn (5 minutes): differentiate \(\mathrm{RSS} = \sum_i (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1x_i)^2\) with respect to \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\), set both to zero, and derive the two formulas
A short derivation that students do in pairs; all it needs is the chain rule.
These are the marks of slide 5, now used together.
Beyond the slide: the derivation \(\partial\mathrm{RSS}/\partial\beta_0 = -2\sum_i (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1x_i) = 0\) gives \(n\beta_0 = \sum y_i - \beta_1\sum x_i\), so \(\beta_0 = \bar y - \beta_1\bar x\).
\(\partial\mathrm{RSS}/\partial\beta_1 = -2\sum_i x_i(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1x_i) = 0\). Substitute \(\beta_0\): \(\sum_i x_i\,[(y_i - \bar y) - \beta_1(x_i - \bar x)] = 0\). Since \(\sum_i \bar x (y_i - \bar y) = 0\) and \(\sum_i \bar x (x_i - \bar x) = 0\), \(x_i\) can be replaced by \(x_i - \bar x\), giving \(\beta_1 = \sum(x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y) / \sum(x_i - \bar x)^2\).
Symbols
\(\bar x\), \(\bar y\) Averages of the inputs and of the outputs. \(\sum_i\) Sum over all data points \(i = 1, \dots, n\). Calibration: the result# \(\hat V = 2.5 + 9.83\,T\)
The least-squares line for the 20 readings.
Sensitivity: \(\hat\beta_1 = 9.83\) mV/\(^\circ\)C
Close to the datasheet value of 10. Whether 9.83 is consistent with 10 is the question of slide 11.
Offset: \(\hat\beta_0 = 2.5\) mV. The datasheet says 0. Is 2.5 a real offset?
The estimate is not exactly zero, but every estimate from noisy data differs a little from the truth. Slide 12 tests it.
Using the calibration: the sensor reads \(V = 500\) mV. Invert the line: \(T = (V - \hat\beta_0)/\hat\beta_1 = (500 - 2.5)/9.83 \approx 50.6~^\circ\)C
The purpose of calibration: turn a raw sensor reading into a temperature. With the datasheet formula (\(T = V/10\)) the answer would be 50.0 \(^\circ\)C; the calibration corrects it by 0.6 \(^\circ\)C.
From the data: \(\bar T = 47.7~^\circ\)C, \(\bar V = 471.6\) mV
The averages used in the formulas of slide 9.
Worked numbers
From the notebook: \(\sum(T_i - \bar T)(V_i - \bar V) = 154\,992.3\) and \(\sum(T_i - \bar T)^2 = 15\,764.0\).
\(\hat\beta_1 = 154\,992.3 / 15\,764.0 = 9.832\) mV/\(^\circ\)C.
\(\hat\beta_0 = 471.64 - 9.832 \times 47.71 = 471.64 - 469.09 = 2.55 \approx 2.5\) mV (2.54 with unrounded averages).
Inversion: \((500 - 2.54)/9.832 = 497.46/9.832 = 50.6~^\circ\)C.
Example: calibrating a pressure sensor# Five readings give the sensor voltage \(V\) (mV) at reference pressures \(P\) (kPa):
\(P\) 0 25 50 75 100 \(V\) 2.1 51.8 101.0 150.6 199.5 Find the least-squares line \(\hat V = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 P\), then the pressure for a reading of \(V = 120\) mV.
Solution triple-click to reveal Averages: \(\bar P = 50\) kPa, \(\bar V = 101.0\) mV.
\[ \sum_i (P_i - \bar P)(V_i - \bar V) = 12340, \qquad \sum_i (P_i - \bar P)^2 = 6250 \]so \(\hat\beta_1 = 12340/6250 = 1.9744\) mV/kPa and \(\hat\beta_0 = \bar V - \hat\beta_1\bar P = 101.0 - 1.9744 \times 50 = 2.28\) mV.
For \(V = 120\) mV: \(P = (120 - 2.28)/1.9744 = 59.6\) kPa.
How sure are we? Standard error# A standard error turns one estimate into a range: the true value is probably within ±2 SE. 20 other readings would give a slightly different slope. The standard error (SE) measures this spread
If we repeated the calibration with 20 new readings, the noise would be different and so would the slope. The SE is the standard deviation of the slope over many such repetitions. It is the “\(\pm\)” of the result.
\(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1) = \sigma / \sqrt{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2}\): noise divided by the spread of \(x\)
The slope is uncertain when the noise \(\sigma\) is large, and well determined when the \(x\) values are spread out. In practice \(\sigma\) is unknown and is replaced by its estimate, the RSE (slide 14).
95% confidence interval: \(\hat\beta_1 \pm 2\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\)
An interval built this way contains the true value in about 95% of repetitions. (The exact multiplier is 2.10 for 18 degrees of freedom; 2 is the usual rounded value.)
The second line is the honest meaning of “95%”: it is a property of the method, over many repeats, not a probability for this one interval.
Calibration data: SE = 0.13 mV/\(^\circ\)C; \(\beta_1 = 9.83 \pm 0.13\) mV/\(^\circ\)C; 95% interval \([9.58, 10.09]\). The datasheet value, 10, is inside
The measured sensitivity is consistent with the datasheet: 9.83 is only \(0.17/0.13 = 1.3\) standard errors below 10.
Smaller SE: less noise; more data; wider range of \(x\)
Three ways to a more precise calibration: a quieter sensor or averaging, more readings, and readings spread over the whole working range. Notebook questions 3 and 4 show the effects.
Symbols
SE Standard error: the standard deviation of an estimate over repeated experiments. \(\sigma\) Standard deviation of the noise \(\varepsilon\) (here truly 15 mV). Worked numbers
\(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1) = \mathrm{RSE}/\sqrt{15\,764.0} = 15.92/125.55 = 0.127\) mV/\(^\circ\)C.
Interval: \(9.832 - 2 \times 0.127 = 9.58\); \(9.832 + 2 \times 0.127 = 10.09\).
Beyond the slide: SE of the intercept \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_0)^2 = \sigma^2\,[1/n + \bar x^2/\sum(x_i - \bar x)^2]\). Here \(15.92^2 \times (1/20 + 47.71^2/15\,764.0) = 253.4 \times (0.05 + 0.1444) = 49.3\), so \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_0) = 7.0\) mV (slide 12). The intercept is uncertain because the data are far from \(T = 0\).
Is the effect real? The \(t\)-statistic# Test the idea “no effect”: is the true coefficient 0? \(t\) = estimate / standard error \(= \hat\beta_1/\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\)
The \(t\)-statistic measures how many standard errors the estimate is away from zero.
\(t\) counts how many standard errors the estimate is away from 0. \(\vert t\vert \) large (more than about 2): the effect is real. \(\vert t\vert \) small: the estimate could be 0 plus noise
If the true value were zero, an estimate more than about 2 SE away would be rare: the 95% interval of slide 11 would not contain 0.
Calibration data: sensitivity \(t = 9.83/0.13 = 77.5\); offset \(t = 2.5/7.0 = 0.36\). The sensitivity is 77 standard errors from 0. The offset is less than one
The two numbers show the two outcomes: one clearly real, one indistinguishable from zero.
A negative \(t\) is just as strong evidence as a positive one; only the size matters. “Null hypothesis” is the name statistics books use for the “no effect” idea.
Worked numbers
Offset: \(t = 2.54/7.02 = 0.36\). Sensitivity: \(t = 9.832/0.1268 = 77.5\).
Example: the t-statistic of the sensitivity# The calibration gives the sensitivity \(\hat\beta_1 = 9.83\) mV/°C with standard error \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1) = 0.12\) mV/°C. (a) Test \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\). (b) Is the datasheet value of 10 mV/°C consistent with the data?
Solution triple-click to reveal (a) \(t = \hat\beta_1/\mathrm{SE} = 9.83/0.12 = 81.9\). This is enormous (anything beyond about 2 is significant at 5%): the sensor certainly responds to temperature.
(b) Test against 10 instead of 0: \(t = (9.83 - 10)/0.12 = -1.42\). \(|t| < 2\), so the difference from the datasheet is within the noise. A 95% interval is \(9.83 \pm 2 \times 0.12 = [9.59, 10.07]\), which contains 10.
The \(p\)-value# value SE \(t\) \(p\) offset 2.5 7.0 0.36 0.72 sensitivity 9.83 0.13 77.5 \(\approx 0\) \(p\)-value: if there were no effect, the chance of getting a \(\vert t\vert \) at least this large from noise alone
Computed from the \(t\) distribution with \(n - 2\) degrees of freedom. A small \(p\) means the data are hard to explain without the effect.
Small \(p\): noise alone rarely does this, so the effect is probably real. \(p < 0.05\): we call the effect significant
A convention, not a law of nature.
Careful: \(p\) is not the chance that the effect is zero. A large \(p\) means “no evidence”, not “no effect”
The most common misreading. “Not significant” means “the data cannot tell it apart from zero”, not “it is zero”. With only three readings almost nothing is significant, however real.
Table: offset 2.5, SE 7.0, \(t = 0.36\), \(p = 0.72\); sensitivity 9.83, SE 0.13, \(t = 77.5\), \(p \approx 0\)
The sensitivity is 77 standard errors from zero: certainly real (of course; the sensor responds to temperature). The offset is only 0.36 standard errors from zero: an offset of 2.5 mV is exactly what noise alone would often produce.
Sensitivity: certainly real. Offset: could be zero, as the datasheet says
Conclusion of the calibration: the sensor meets its datasheet within the uncertainty.
Symbols
\(t\) Estimate divided by its standard error. \(p\) Probability of \(\vert t\vert \) at least this large if the true coefficient were 0. How not to read a p-value. xkcd #1478 “P-Values” by Randall Munroe, CC BY-NC 2.5. Hover for the alt text. How good is the fit? RSE and \(R^2\)# R² compares the spread left around the line (RSS) with the spread around the average (TSS). Residual standard error: the typical size of a residual. \(\mathrm{RSE} = \sqrt{\mathrm{RSS}/(n-2)}\)
The RSE estimates the noise \(\sigma\). We divide by \(n - 2\), not \(n\), because two coefficients were estimated from the same data, which makes the residuals slightly smaller than the true errors.
\(R^2\): the fraction of the variation in \(Y\) that the model explains. \(R^2 = 1 - \mathrm{RSS}/\mathrm{TSS}\), \(\mathrm{TSS} = \sum_i (y_i - \bar y)^2\)
TSS (total sum of squares) is the variation of \(y\) around its average, before using \(x\). RSS is what is left after the fit. Their ratio is the fraction unexplained.
\(R^2 = 0\): explains nothing. \(R^2 = 1\): perfect
\(R^2\) has no units, which makes it easy to compare between problems.
Calibration data: RSE = 15.9 mV, about 1.6 \(^\circ\)C. \(R^2 = 0.997\): temperature explains 99.7% of the variation in the output
The RSE is close to the true noise, 15 mV. Divided by the sensitivity, \(15.9/9.83 = 1.6~^\circ\)C: a single reading of this sensor is uncertain by about \(\pm1.6~^\circ\)C. \(R^2 = 0.997\): temperature explains 99.7% of the variation in the output.
A “good” \(R^2\) depends on the field: a calibration expects more than 0.99
A calibration with \(R^2 = 0.9\) would mean a faulty sensor. A model of household electricity use from survey data with \(R^2 = 0.5\) may be excellent, because people are unpredictable.
Symbols
RSE Residual standard error (units of \(y\)). TSS Total sum of squares, \(\sum(y_i - \bar y)^2\). \(R^2\) Fraction of the variation explained, between 0 and 1. Worked numbers
\(\mathrm{RSS} = \mathrm{RSE}^2 \times (n - 2) = 15.92^2 \times 18 = 4562\) mV\(^2\). \(\mathrm{TSS} = 1\,528\,457\) mV\(^2\), so \(R^2 = 1 - 4562/1\,528\,457 = 1 - 0.0030 = 0.997\).
Example: RSE and R² from the sums# A fit to \(n = 20\) calibration readings has \(\mathrm{RSS} = 4480\) mV² and total sum of squares \(\mathrm{TSS} = \sum(y_i - \bar y)^2 = 1\,515\,000\) mV². Compute the residual standard error and \(R^2\).
Solution triple-click to reveal \[ \mathrm{RSE} = \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{n-2}} = \sqrt{\frac{4480}{18}} = 15.8\ \mathrm{mV}, \qquad R^2 = 1 - \frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{\mathrm{TSS}} = 1 - \frac{4480}{1\,515\,000} = 0.9970. \]A typical reading lies about 15.8 mV from the line, and the line explains 99.70% of the variation in the voltage.

title: The maximal margin classifier
content:
The maximal margin classifier# Example: has water been added to the milk?# Milk testing has a long history (a dairy-school laboratory, 1890s). Today an instrument and a classifier can do it. Photo: Unknown authorUnknown author, Wikimedia Commons, Public domain Adding water to milk lowers its density (g/mL); lowers its electrical conductivity (mS/cm), because the salts are diluted
Water (1.000 g/mL) is lighter than milk (about 1.030), so each 10% of added water lowers the density by about 0.003 g/mL. Milk's conductivity comes from dissolved salts; diluting them lowers it. Milk adulteration was named in the class survey.
Two inputs, both measured with cheap instruments (a lactometer and a conductivity probe). Output: pure or adulterated
A lactometer is a hydrometer calibrated for milk, used at collection centres.
Two datasets: A: 30 samples, classes clearly apart (used first). B: 200 samples, classes overlap (used for the soft margin)
In A the watered samples have more water added, so the classes separate completely. A is used on slide 8, B on slides 11–12.
Inputs are standardised: mean 0, standard deviation 1
Density varies by thousandths, conductivity by tenths; without standardising, distances would be dominated by conductivity.
A hyperplane# With two inputs, a hyperplane is a straight line: \(\beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 + \beta_2X_2 = 0\). With \(p\) inputs it is a flat surface of dimension \(p - 1\)
In three dimensions a hyperplane is an ordinary plane.
Classify by the sign: \(\beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 > 0\): one class; \(< 0\): the other
The line divides the plane into two half-planes.
Size tells confidence: the farther a point is from the line, the more sure we are of its class
If \(\beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2 = 1\), the value \(\beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2\) is exactly the signed distance from the line.
If the classes can be separated at all, there are infinitely many separating lines. Which one?
Symbols
\(\beta_0, \beta_1, \beta_2\) Coefficients of the line. \(X_1, X_2\) The two inputs (standardised density and conductivity). Example: which side of the hyperplane?# A classifier for milk uses the hyperplane \(-3 + x_1 + 2x_2 = 0\), with \(x_1\) the conductivity and \(x_2\) the density reading (both standardised); positive values mean “water added”. Classify the samples \((1, 0.5)\), \((2, 1.0)\) and \((3, 1.5)\).
Solution triple-click to reveal Evaluate \(f(x) = -3 + x_1 + 2x_2\):
\((1, 0.5)\): \(f = -1.0\): pure. \((2, 1.0)\): \(f = +1.0\): water added. \((3, 1.5)\): \(f = +3.0\): water added. The size of \(f\) also matters: the further from 0, the further the sample lies from the boundary, and the more confident the classification.
The maximal margin classifier# The maximal margin classifier puts the widest possible street between the two classes. Margin: the distance from the line to the nearest point. Choose the line with the largest margin: the widest “street” between the classes
Support vectors: the points on the edge of the street. They alone fix the line
They “support” the street, like posts.
Why the widest street? A new sample near the boundary is less likely to fall on the wrong side
Solved as an optimisation problem: find the \(\beta\)'s that make the margin as large as possible (ISLP 9.1.4)
Maximise \(M\) subject to \(\sum_j\beta_j^2 = 1\) and \(y_i(\beta_0 + \beta_1x_{i1} + \dots) \ge M\) for every \(i\), with \(y_i = \pm1\).
Symbols
\(M\) Margin: half the street width. \(y_i\) Class of point \(i\) coded as \(+1\) or \(-1\). Example: the width of the street# A maximal margin classifier is written \(\beta_0 + \boldsymbol\beta\cdot\mathbf x = 0\) with the support vectors on \(\beta_0 + \boldsymbol\beta\cdot\mathbf x = \pm 1\). If \(\boldsymbol\beta = (3, 4)\), how wide is the margin (the street between the two classes)?
Solution triple-click to reveal The distance between the parallel lines \(\boldsymbol\beta\cdot\mathbf x + \beta_0 = +1\) and \(= -1\) is \(2/\|\boldsymbol\beta\|\):
\[ \|\boldsymbol\beta\| = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5, \qquad \text{width} = 2/5 = 0.4. \]The SVM maximises this width, which is the same as minimising \(\|\boldsymbol\beta\|\).
Dataset A: the widest street# Solid: the maximal margin line. Dashed: the edges of the street
scikit-learn writes the line as \(w_1z_1 + w_2z_2 + b = 0\) and the edges as \(= \pm1\). Here \(w = (-0.966, -0.664)\), \(b = -0.318\).
3 support vectors (circled) out of 30 samples
Two on one edge and one on the other, the minimum needed to fix a line in two dimensions.
Street width: 1.71 (standardised units, i.e. standard deviations)
The distance between the two edges is \(2/\Vert w\Vert \).
Move any other point (without crossing the street): the line does not change
This is different from logistic regression, where every point pulls on the fit. Notebook question 1 tests it.
Symbols
\(w\), \(b\) scikit-learn's coefficients and intercept. \(\Vert w\Vert \) Length of \(w\), \(\sqrt{w_1^2 + w_2^2}\). Worked numbers
\(\Vert w\Vert = \sqrt{0.966^2 + 0.664^2} = \sqrt{0.933 + 0.441} = 1.172\); width \(= 2/1.172 = 1.71\).

title: About the course
content:

Google Classroom is the single official place for the course.
Course registration on the UoN student portal is mandatory before you can sit the CAT and the examination
A student who is not registered cannot be examined, whatever work they have done.
Attendance is mandatory and is recorded in every class, online and physical
Attendance is taken in both modes.
