title: Generative models: LDA, QDA, naive Bayes
content:
Generative models: LDA, QDA, naive Bayes# Probability words for the next four slides# Word Meaning \(\Pr(A \mid B)\) probability of \(A\) given that \(B\) is true (conditional probability) prior \(\pi_k\) probability of class \(k\) before we look at \(X\): how common the class is density \(f_k(x)\) how the inputs \(X\) are spread in class \(k\): high where class-\(k\) points are common normal (Gaussian) the bell-shaped distribution, set by its mean and spread mean \(\mu\) (“mu”) the centre of a distribution: the average covariance \(\Sigma\) (capital “sigma”, here not a sum) the spread of each input and how inputs vary together: it sets the size, shape and tilt of the cloud of points LDA, QDA and naive Bayes are described in the language of probability. Most students have met these words in a statistics course but may not be fluent. Go through them before the formulas.
\(\Pr(A \mid B)\): probability of \(A\) given that \(B\) is true (conditional probability)
For example, \(\Pr(\text{faulty} \mid v = 6~\text{mm/s})\): among machines vibrating at 6 mm/s, the fraction that are faulty.
Prior \(\pi_k\): probability of class \(k\) before we look at \(X\): how common the class is
If 30% of machines in the plant are faulty, the prior for “faulty” is 0.3.
Density \(f_k(x)\): how the inputs \(X\) are spread in class \(k\): high where class-\(k\) points are common
For one input, think of a smoothed histogram of the readings from that class.
Normal (Gaussian): the bell-shaped distribution, set by its mean and spread. Mean \(\mu\) (“mu”): the centre of a distribution: the average
Covariance \(\Sigma\) (capital “sigma”, here not a sum): the spread of each input and how inputs vary together: it sets the size, shape and tilt of the cloud of points
With two inputs it is a \(2 \times 2\) table: the two variances on the diagonal and the covariance (which sets the correlation) off it. Warn students that the same Greek letter \(\Sigma\) also means “sum”; the context tells which.
Bayes' theorem turns “how \(X\) looks in each class” into “which class, given \(X\)”
The next slide gives the formula.
Another route: model each class# Generative classifiers model how each class is spread, then pick the class whose curve is higher. Logistic regression models \(\Pr(Y = k \mid X)\) directly
It is called a discriminative method: it only describes the boundary between classes.
Instead, describe how \(X\) is spread in each class, then use Bayes' theorem: \(\Pr(Y = k \mid X = x) = \pi_kf_k(x)/\sum_l \pi_lf_l(x)\)
A generative method describes each class fully: what healthy machines look like, what faulty ones look like, and how common each is. Bayes' theorem then turns this into the probability of each class for a given machine.
Predict the class with the largest probability
This is the Bayes classifier of Lecture 1, with estimated ingredients.
Two ingredients: \(\pi_k\) (“pi”), fraction of class \(k\) in the training data; \(f_k(x)\), how \(X\) is distributed in class \(k\)
The methods on the next slides differ only in how they estimate \(f_k\).
Machines: \(\hat\pi_{\text{faulty}} = 122/400 = 0.305\), \(\hat\pi_{\text{healthy}} = 0.695\)
The prior: before looking at the sensors, a machine is faulty with probability 0.305.
Symbols
\(k\) Class label. \(\pi_k\) Prior probability of class \(k\). \(f_k(x)\) Probability density of the inputs in class \(k\). \(\sum_l\) Sum over all classes. Worked numbers
Bayes' theorem for one machine: if \(f_{\text{faulty}}(x) = 0.02\) and \(f_{\text{healthy}}(x) = 0.01\) (made-up densities), then \(\Pr(\text{faulty} \mid x) = 0.305 \times 0.02/(0.305 \times 0.02 + 0.695 \times 0.01) = 0.0061/0.01305 = 0.47\). Although the reading is twice as typical of faulty machines, the prior tips the decision to healthy.
Linear discriminant analysis (LDA)# Assume each class is a normal (Gaussian) cloud: each class has its own mean \(\mu_k\); all classes share the same spread and shape (covariance \(\Sigma\))
Picture each class as an elliptical cloud of points. LDA allows the clouds to sit in different places but insists they have the same size, shape and tilt.
Then the boundary between classes is a straight line
With equal covariances, the quadratic terms in \(x\) cancel in the ratio of the two densities, leaving a linear boundary (ESL 4.3).
Machines: class means: healthy \(v = 2.5\) mm/s, \(T = 50.0~^\circ\)C; faulty \(v = 4.7\) mm/s, \(T = 60.8~^\circ\)C
Estimated from the training data. (True: 2.5, 50 and 4.5, 60.)
LDA or logistic? Both give a straight-line boundary. LDA is more stable when classes are well separated or data are few
When classes are perfectly separated, logistic coefficients blow up (slide 33); LDA does not. When the Gaussian assumption is badly wrong, logistic regression is safer.
Symbols
\(\mu_k\) Mean of the inputs in class \(k\). \(\Sigma\) Covariance matrix: spreads and correlations of the inputs. QDA: each class has its own shape# Quadratic discriminant analysis: each class has its own covariance \(\Sigma_k\)
The clouds may now have different sizes and tilts.
The boundary becomes a curve. More parameters to estimate: needs more data
With two inputs, each covariance has three numbers (two spreads and a correlation). QDA estimates one per class; LDA one in total. With many inputs the difference is large: \(p(p + 1)/2\) per class.
Faulty machines vary much more than healthy ones, so QDA suits them
In the simulation, faulty machines have about twice the spread and a strong correlation; healthy ones have neither.
Plot: black, logistic boundary; red, QDA boundary
The QDA boundary curves around the compact healthy cloud.
Symbols
\(\Sigma_k\) Covariance matrix of class \(k\). Naive Bayes# Assume the inputs are independent within each class: \(f_k(x) = f_{k1}(x_1) \times \dots \times f_{kp}(x_p)\)
Instead of a joint distribution for all inputs, estimate one simple distribution per input per class, and multiply.
Only one-dimensional distributions to estimate: works with many inputs and little data. The assumption is usually false, but the method often still works
The probabilities it gives may be poor, but the ranking of classes is often right, which is all a classifier needs.
Why “naive”: in faulty machines, vibration and temperature rise together. Naive Bayes ignores this
The correlation of 0.8 in faulty machines is thrown away.
Where it shines: spam filters and text: thousands of inputs (words), each simple on its own
Symbols
\(f_{kj}(x_j)\) Distribution of input \(j\) in class \(k\). Comparing classifiers on the test machines# Method test error AUC Always say “healthy” 0.296 0.50 Logistic regression 0.113 0.890 LDA 0.118 0.889 QDA 0.110 0.906 Naive Bayes 0.116 0.885 KNN, \(K = 1\) 0.170 0.797 KNN, \(K = 15\) 0.112 0.885 Table: always “healthy” 0.296, AUC 0.50; logistic 0.113, 0.890; LDA 0.118, 0.889; QDA 0.110, 0.906; naive Bayes 0.116, 0.885; KNN \(K = 1\) 0.170, 0.797; KNN \(K = 15\) 0.112, 0.885. Test error \(= 1 -\) accuracy. KNN on standardised inputs
All fitted on the same 400 training machines and scored on the same 2000 test machines, as in ISLP Section 4.5. The first row is the baseline: 593 of 2000 machines are faulty, so always saying “healthy” is wrong \(593/2000 = 29.6\%\) of the time.
All good methods reach about 11% error
The overlap of the classes sets a floor that no method can beat.
QDA is best: the classes really have different shapes
Its assumption matches how the data were generated.
KNN with \(K = 1\) overfits: training error 0, test error 0.17
Each training machine is its own nearest neighbour, so training error is zero; on new machines the boundary follows noise (Lecture 1).
No method wins everywhere. Compare on test data
On another dataset the order may be reversed.
More than two classes# With \(K\) classes, each class \(k\) gets its own line \(z_k = \beta_{0k} + \beta_{1k}X_1 + \dots\)
Note: here \(K\) is the number of classes, not the number of neighbours as in KNN.
Softmax turns the \(K\) numbers into probabilities: \(\Pr(Y = k \mid X) = e^{z_k}/(e^{z_1} + \dots + e^{z_K})\)
Exponentials make every number positive; dividing by the sum makes them add up to 1. With \(K = 2\) it reduces to the sigmoid.
All probabilities are positive and add up to 1. Predict the class with the largest
Fault type: imbalance, misalignment or bearing wear? Three classes, three lines, one softmax
LDA, QDA, naive Bayes and KNN handle \(K\) classes directly. Softmax is the last layer of most neural-network classifiers (Lecture 7)
Worked numbers
If \(z = (2, 1, 0)\): \(e^2 = 7.39\), \(e^1 = 2.72\), \(e^0 = 1\); sum 11.11. Probabilities \(0.665\), \(0.245\), \(0.090\).
Things to watch# Rare classes: if 99% of machines are healthy, “always say healthy” is 99% accurate and useless. Look at recall and precision, not only accuracy
In real plants faults are rare, so this matters.
Standardise for KNN: distances mix mm/s and \(^\circ\)C. Standardising lowers the KNN (\(K = 15\)) error from 0.120 to 0.112
Temperatures vary by about 7.6 \(^\circ\)C, vibrations by about 1.5 mm/s; unscaled, the distance is dominated by temperature. Logistic regression and LDA are not affected by scaling.
Curved boundaries: use QDA, or add inputs such as \(x^2\) or \(x_1x_2\) to logistic regression
As in Lecture 2.
Perfectly separated classes: logistic coefficients grow without limit. Regularisation (Lecture 4) fixes this
If a line separates the classes perfectly, the likelihood keeps improving as the S-curve becomes a sharper step.
Judge on test data, never on the training data
Summary# Logistic regression: \(p = \sigma(\beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 + \dots)\); the log-odds is linear; fit by maximum likelihood A threshold turns a probability into a decision; its choice trades missed faults against false alarms Judge a classifier with the confusion matrix, recall, precision and the ROC curve, on test data LDA, QDA and naive Bayes model each class, then use Bayes' theorem Try several methods and compare them on the same test data Ask students to state each point in their own words.
Before next class# Read ISLP Chapter 4 (4.1–4.5) Run lecture03_classification.ipynb in Google Colab: fit the motors, draw the ROC curve, and compare the five classifiers Group: load your project dataset in Colab. Report its size, its inputs and its output, and fit a first linear or logistic regression The first real step of the project: a working baseline.
Next class: resampling and regularisation: cross-validation, the bootstrap, ridge and lasso
ISLP Chapters 5–6: how to estimate the test error when there is no separate test set, and how to control complexity.

title: Gradient descent
content:
Gradient descent# Loss and cost: what is the difference?# Two words that students will meet in every later lecture and in every software library, often used loosely. Fix them now.
Loss: how wrong the model is on one data point. \(\ell_i = \frac12(y_i - \hat y_i)^2\)
The loss is a number for a single reading: half its squared residual.
Cost: the average loss over all \(n\) points. One number for the whole dataset. \(J(\bb) = \frac1n\sum_i\ell_i = \frac{1}{2n}\sum_i (y_i - \hat y_i)^2\)
The cost scores a whole set of coefficients. Dividing by \(n\) keeps the numbers of a similar size whatever the data size; the \(\frac12\) cancels the 2 that appears when we differentiate.
Training = finding the \(\bb\) with the smallest cost
This sentence is true for every model in the course: only the form of the loss changes (cross-entropy in Lecture 3, for example).
Cost \(= \mathrm{RSS}/2n\), so the best line is the same. Many books say “loss” for both
Dividing by a fixed number does not move the minimum. ISLP and PyTorch use “loss” for both meanings; in this course loss is for one point and cost for the average.
Example: 3 points with residuals \(1, -2, 3\): losses \(0.5, 2, 4.5\); cost \(J = (0.5 + 2 + 4.5)/3 = 2.33\)
Worked numbers
Losses: \(\frac12 \times 1^2 = 0.5\), \(\frac12 \times (-2)^2 = 2\), \(\frac12 \times 3^2 = 4.5\). RSS \(= 1 + 4 + 9 = 14\), and \(\mathrm{RSS}/2n = 14/6 = 2.33\), the same number.
Gradient descent: walk downhill# Gradient descent walks downhill on the cost. The step size decides whether it crawls, runs, or flies off. Start with any \(\bb\). Repeat: \(\bb_{\text{new}} = \bb_{\text{old}} - \alpha\,\nabla J\). Stop when the cost \(J\) no longer falls
The gradient \(\nabla J\) points uphill; a step against it goes downhill. \(\alpha\) sets the size of the step. The cost is the one of the previous slide.
\(\alpha\) is our first example of a setting that is chosen rather than fitted (a hyperparameter, Lecture 4).
Why learn this? Most later models (logistic regression, neural networks) have no formula. Gradient descent works for all of them
For linear regression the normal equations already give the answer. We learn gradient descent here because the answer is known, so we can see it work.
Plot: a bowl-shaped cost; big steps where it is steep, small steps near the bottom
The step is \(\alpha\) times the slope, so the steps shrink automatically as the slope flattens near the minimum.
Symbols
\(J(\bb)\) Cost of the coefficients \(\bb\). \(\alpha\) Step size (learning rate). \(\nabla J\) Gradient: the vector of partial derivatives \(\partial J/\partial\beta_j\). What is the gradient \(\nabla J\)?# One coefficient: \(\nabla J\) is the ordinary derivative \(dJ/d\beta\). Slope negative: the cost falls to the right, so increase \(\beta\). Slope positive: decrease \(\beta\). The minus sign in the update does this
Draw a parabola at the board, mark a point to the left of the minimum, and show that the slope there is negative, so \(-\alpha \times\) slope is a step to the right, towards the minimum.
Many coefficients: a list of slopes, one per coefficient: \(\nabla J = (\partial J/\partial\beta_0, \partial J/\partial\beta_1, \dots, \partial J/\partial\beta_p)\)
Each partial derivative is the slope when only that coefficient changes and the others are held fixed. Together they point in the steepest uphill direction.
The plot on the last slide: \(J = (\beta - 2)^2\), \(\alpha = 0.2\). Slope \(dJ/d\beta = 2(\beta - 2)\); at \(\beta = 0\) it is \(-4\). \(\beta_{\text{new}} = 0 - 0.2 \times (-4) = 0.8\). Next: \(0.8 + 0.2 \times 2.4 = 1.28\), … \(\to 2\)
These are exactly the red points of the previous slide.
Worked numbers
At \(\beta = 0.8\): slope \(2(0.8 - 2) = -2.4\), so \(\beta = 0.8 + 0.2 \times 2.4 = 1.28\). At 1.28: slope \(-1.44\), \(\beta = 1.568\). Each step removes 40% of the remaining distance to 2, because \(\beta - 2\) is multiplied by \(1 - 2\alpha = 0.6\).
Gradient descent for linear regression# Batch (all data points in each step): \(\bb \leftarrow \bb + \frac{\alpha}{n}\bX\T(\by - \bX\bb)\)
For the cost of slide 25, \(\nabla J = -\frac1n\bX\T(\by - \bX\bb)\). Substituting gives this update. \(\by - \bX\bb\) is the column of residuals.
Stochastic (one point \(i\) in each step): \(\bb \leftarrow \bb + \alpha(y_i - \hat y_i)x_i\)
Use one data point at a time, cycling through the data. Each step is cheap; used for very large datasets and for neural networks.
As in a program: compute the right-hand side, then store it in \(\bb\).
Read the update: the step is proportional to the error \(y_i - \hat y_i\). Big mistake: big correction. Small mistake: small correction
When a prediction is too low, the coefficients move so as to raise it, in proportion to the input values.
Good news: the cost is a single bowl. Downhill always leads to the one best answer
\(J\) is a quadratic function of \(\bb\) (a convex bowl), so there is only one minimum. Neural networks do not have this property.
Symbols
\(\leftarrow\) Assignment: replace the old value. \(x_i\) Row \(i\) of \(\bX\) (with the 1 for the intercept). Example: one step of gradient descent by hand# Fit \(y = \beta x\) (no intercept) to the points \((1, 2.2), (2, 3.9), (3, 6.1)\) with cost \(J(\beta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (y_i - \beta x_i)^2\). Start at \(\beta = 1\) with step size \(\alpha = 0.05\). Do one gradient-descent step. What is the exact minimiser?
Solution triple-click to reveal \[ \frac{dJ}{d\beta} = -\frac{2}{n}\sum_i x_i (y_i - \beta x_i) = -\frac{2}{3}\big[1(1.2) + 2(1.9) + 3(3.1)\big] = -9.533 \]Update: \(\beta \leftarrow 1 - 0.05 \times (-9.533) = 1.4767\).
Exact minimiser (set the derivative to zero): \(\beta = \sum x_i y_i / \sum x_i^2 = 28.3/14 = 2.0214\). One step moved from 1 to 1.4767, towards 2.0214.
Choosing the step size \(\alpha\)# Plot: cost against step for \(\alpha = 0.01\), 0.5 and 2.1. Calibration data (temperature standardised), 40 steps
Gradient descent on the sensor data of slide 10, starting from \(\bb = 0\) (cost \(1.49 \times 10^5\) mV\(^2\)). The vertical axis is logarithmic.
Too small (grey): very slow
With \(\alpha = 0.01\) the cost has only fallen to \(6.7 \times 10^4\) mV\(^2\) after 40 steps.
About right (green): done in about 10 steps
With \(\alpha = 0.5\) the cost reaches its minimum, 114 mV\(^2\), by step 10, and the coefficients equal the least-squares values (\(9.832\) mV/\(^\circ\)C and \(2.54\) mV).
Too large (red): overshoots and blows up
With \(\alpha = 2.1\) each step jumps past the minimum to a higher point on the other side; the cost grows without limit.
Always: plot the cost at every step. It must go down
The simplest check that the code and the step size are right.
Worked numbers
Minimum cost \(= \mathrm{RSS}/(2n) = 4562/40 = 114\) mV\(^2\). Cost at steps 0, 1, 2, 3 with \(\alpha = 0.5\): 149 435; 37 444; 9 447; 2 447 mV\(^2\) — about four times smaller each step. With standardised input, \(\bX\T\bX/n\) is the identity, so \(\alpha = 1\) would reach the minimum in one step, and any \(\alpha > 2\) diverges.
Try it. Try \(\alpha = 0.1\), then \(0.9\), then \(1.05\). Small steps are slow, steps near 1 zig-zag, and steps above 1 diverge. Scale the inputs first# Raw temperatures (6 to 93 \(^\circ\)C): only tiny steps are possible; after 5000 steps, the offset is still wrong (1.4 instead of 2.5 mV)
With raw inputs, the cost bowl is a long narrow valley: very steep across the slope direction (temperatures are large numbers) and very flat along the intercept direction. A step size small enough not to blow up across the valley (at most \(6.5 \times 10^{-4}\)) is far too small to move along it.
Standardise each input: \(z = (x - \bar x)/s\). Every input now has mean 0 and spread 1; about 10 steps are enough
Subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation. All directions of the bowl become equally steep.
Rule: standardise before gradient descent. Use the mean and \(s\) of the training data only
Test data must be scaled with the training mean and \(s\), so that no information about the test data leaks into training.
Sensor data: inputs often differ by many orders of magnitude (W/m\(^2\), \(^\circ\)C, mV, kHz). Scaling is a routine first step
In the solar data, \(G\) is in hundreds and \(T\) in tens; in a vibration dataset, frequencies may be in kHz.
Symbols
\(z\) Standardised input. \(s\) Standard deviation of the input (28.1 \(^\circ\)C for the calibration temperatures). Worked numbers
After fitting on \(z\), convert back: slope per \(^\circ\)C \(= \beta_z/s = 276.03/28.075 = 9.832\) mV/\(^\circ\)C; offset \(= \beta_{0z} - 9.832 \times 47.71 = 471.64 - 469.10 = 2.54\) mV.
Things to check# Problem Sign Fix Curved relation residuals form a curve add \(x^2\), or transform Noise grows residuals fan out transform \(y\); weighted fit Outlier one very large residual check it; do not just delete it Correlated inputs large SE, strange signs drop or combine inputs Curved relation: residuals form a curve; fix: add \(x^2\), or transform
Plot the residuals against the fitted values or each input. A U-shape means the straight line misses a curve.
Noise grows: residuals fan out; fix: transform \(y\); weighted fit
Unequal noise (heteroscedasticity) makes the SEs wrong.
Outlier: one very large residual; fix: check it; do not just delete it
It may be a recording error, or the most interesting point in the dataset (a sensor starting to fail).
Correlated inputs: large SE, strange signs; fix: drop or combine inputs
Collinearity (ISLP 3.3.3): when inputs move together, the data cannot separate their effects, as on slide 20.
Always plot the residuals. \(R^2\) and \(p\)-values alone can hide all of these problems
The notebook's residual plot for the solar panel shows the dusty panels below zero: the missing input shows up in the residuals.
Summary# Least squares chooses the line with the smallest RSS SE, \(t\) and \(p\) say how much to trust each coefficient; RSE and \(R^2\) say how well the model fits Many inputs: \(\bX\T\bX\,\hat\bb = \bX\T\by\). Each coefficient holds the other inputs fixed Categories enter as dummy variables; products of inputs give interactions Gradient descent finds the same answer step by step; standardise first and watch the cost Ask students to state each point in their own words before showing it.
Before next class# Read ISLP Chapter 3 (3.1–3.3) It covers everything in this lecture except gradient descent.
Run lecture02_linear_regression.ipynb in Google Colab: calibrate the sensor, fit the solar panel, and write your own gradient descent Each group works through the notebook and answers its 12 questions.
Group: find a dataset for your project problem and post its source on Google Classroom Possible sources: the groups' own sensor measurements, Kaggle, the UCI Machine Learning Repository, and the Kenya Open Data portal.

title: Introduction to machine learning
content:
Introduction to machine learning# Today# What machine learning is, and why we need it; 2. Representation, evaluation, optimisation; 3. Words, notation and matrix algebra; 4. Types of machine learning; 5. Statistical learning: estimating \(f\); 6. Assessing model accuracy; 7. The bias–variance trade-off; 8. Classification: Bayes classifier and KNN The plan for the second half of the lecture. Items 5–8 are the core of ISLP Chapter 2 and are used in every later lecture. Item 3 sets out the words and symbols of the whole course, so that no later slide uses a term that has not been defined.
Reading: ISLP Chapter 2 (Statistical Learning). ESL Chapter 2 for the mathematics
ISLP Chapter 2 covers everything in this half of the lecture. ESL Chapter 2 treats the same ideas (least squares, nearest neighbours, the bias–variance trade-off) with more mathematics.
Notebook: lecture01_intro_ml.ipynb on Google Classroom
It reproduces the cooling-curve and KNN ideas of slides 32–39 (its random data differ slightly, so its numbers are close to, not identical with, the slides).
What is machine learning?# Machine learning is the part of artificial intelligence that learns from data; deep learning is the part of machine learning that uses many-layered neural networks. Machine learning (ML) is a subfield of artificial intelligence that lets computers learn from data without being explicitly programmed
Artificial intelligence is the broad goal of making computers do tasks that seem to need intelligence. Machine learning is the part of AI where the computer learns how to do a task from examples, instead of following rules written by a person.
Herbert Simon: “Learning is any process by which a system improves performance from experience.”
Herbert Simon was an American scientist and Nobel laureate in economics, and a founder of AI. His definition applies to people and machines alike: learning means getting better with experience.
Tom Mitchell (1997): a computer program learns from experience \(E\) with respect to a task \(T\) and performance measure \(P\) if its performance on \(T\), measured by \(P\), improves with experience \(E\)
Mitchell's definition makes Simon's precise. To say a program learns, name three things: the task it does (\(T\)), how its success is measured (\(P\)), and the experience it learns from (\(E\), usually data). Learning means that \(P\) improves as \(E\) grows.
Example: \(T\) (task): label a motor as healthy or faulty from its vibration signal. \(P\) (performance): fraction labelled correctly. \(E\) (experience): past vibration records labelled by technicians
A worn bearing or loose mounting changes how a motor vibrates. The task is to label each motor from an accelerometer signal. The performance is the fraction labelled correctly. The experience is past records for which a technician later confirmed whether the motor was healthy or faulty. This is the fault-detection problem several students named in the survey.
Symbols
\(T\) Task: what the program must do. \(P\) Performance measure: how success is scored. \(E\) Experience: the data the program learns from. Is that all there is to it? Not quite, as this course will show. xkcd #1838 “Machine Learning” by Randall Munroe, CC BY-NC 2.5. Hover for the alt text. Why machine learning?# Diagram: traditional programming: data + rules \(\to\) program \(\to\) answers. Machine learning: data + answers \(\to\) learning \(\to\) rules (model)
In traditional programming a person writes the rules, and the computer applies them to data to produce answers. In machine learning we give the computer data together with the correct answers, and it works out the rules itself.
Rules are hard to write by hand. What rule tells a worn bearing from a healthy one in a vibration signal?
An experienced technician can hear a failing bearing, but writing precise rules in terms of thousands of signal samples is almost impossible. Learning from many labelled signals works much better.
Too much data. A factory with hundreds of sensors, each sampled many times per second, produces far more data than anyone can read
For example, 500 sensors sampled 100 times per second give \(500 \times 100 \times 86\,400 \approx 4.3\) billion readings per day. Only an automatic method can watch them all.
Systems change. Detectors age and sensors drift; a learned model can be retrained on new data
Hand-written rules must be rewritten when conditions change; a learned model is simply retrained on new data.
Model: the rules the computer learns; it turns inputs into answers
The word model is used on almost every slide from now on, so it is defined here. Once learned, a model is applied to new data like a traditional program.
ML in a nutshell: three components# Every machine-learning project follows this loop: a question, data, a model, an honest evaluation, then use. Every ML method can be described by three choices. We use this framework in every lecture.
Representation: how do we turn raw data into numbers a model can use? A vibration signal \(\to\) amplitudes at 1000 frequencies. A camera image \(\to\) pixel values. A smart meter \(\to\) kWh used in each hour
A computer model needs numbers. Representation is how raw measurements become a list of numbers for each object. A vibration signal becomes 1000 amplitudes, one per frequency (its Fourier spectrum); an image becomes its pixel values; a smart meter's record becomes 24 numbers per day, the energy used in each hour. The term also covers the family of models we allow, for example all straight lines.
Evaluation: how do we know the model is good? Give it a score: for a number, the average squared error (later today); for a category, the fraction labelled correctly. Always scored on data the model has not seen
We need a number that scores a model. For numerical outputs, the mean squared error (slide 32). For categories, the fraction labelled correctly, called the accuracy (slide 37); Lecture 3 adds other scores. The crucial rule: score the model on new data, not on the data used to train it (slide 34).
Optimisation: how do we find the best model? Change the model's adjustable numbers (its parameters) step by step to reduce the error: gradient descent (Lecture 2). Keep the model simple: regularisation (Lecture 4)
A parameter is a number inside the model that is learned from data, for example the slope of a straight line. Optimisation searches for the parameter values with the best score. Gradient descent repeatedly adjusts the parameters in the direction that reduces the error. Regularisation adds a penalty for complexity so that the model does not fit the noise. Only the names are needed today.
Words we use all through the course# A solar farm. Our first data set: the power of a panel from the sunlight (irradiance) and the panel temperature. Photo: Kkiefuik This photo was taken with Canon EOS 90D, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0 Data as a table: each row is one observation, the input columns form X, the output column is y. Word Meaning Example (solar panel) observation one measured example (also: data point, reading, sample) one reading of the panel input a quantity we measure and use to predict (also: variable, feature, predictor) sunlight, cell temperature output the quantity we want to predict (also: response, target) electrical power label the known, correct output of an observation the power actually measured model the rule that turns inputs into a predicted output power \(\approx\) a formula in sunlight and temperature parameter an adjustable number inside the model, learned from data how many watts per W/m\(^2\) training data observations used to fit the model last month's readings test data new observations kept aside to check the model this week's readings This table collects the everyday words of machine learning in one place. Different books use different words for the same thing, so the table also gives the common alternatives. Go through it quickly, pointing at the solar-panel column; the same panel appears on slides 21, 23 and 25, and again in Lecture 2.
Observation: one measured example (also: data point, reading, sample); example: one reading of the panel
One row of the data table.
Input: a quantity we measure and use to predict (also: variable, feature, predictor); example: sunlight, cell temperature
Statisticians say predictor or independent variable; computer scientists say feature.
Output: the quantity we want to predict (also: response, target); example: electrical power
Also called the dependent variable.
Label: the known, correct output of an observation; example: the power actually measured
In the training data the output is known; that known value is the label. “Labelled data” means data with these known outputs. The word is used most for categories (“healthy”, “faulty”), but it applies to numbers too.
Model: the rule that turns inputs into a predicted output; example: power \(\approx\) a formula in sunlight and temperature
As on slide 17.
Parameter: an adjustable number inside the model, learned from data; example: how many watts per W/m\(^2\)
For the panel, one parameter says how much the power rises for each extra W/m\(^2\) of sunlight.
Training data: observations used to fit the model; example: last month's readings. Test data: new observations kept aside to check the model; example: this week's readings
“Fit” and “train” mean the same thing: choose the parameters from data. The test data are not used in fitting, so they show how the model does on data it has never seen. This split is the subject of slide 34.
Types of machine learning# The main types of machine learning. What the data look like in each type. Type What it learns from Example Supervised labelled data: inputs with their known outputs predict a building's electricity use (kWh) from temperature and time of day Unsupervised unlabelled data: inputs only; find groups or structure group smart-meter customers by their daily load profile, with no labels given Reinforcement trial and error: actions earn rewards from an environment learn when to switch a heater on and off to hold a room at a set temperature Supervised: labelled data: inputs with their known outputs. Example: predict a building's electricity use (kWh) from temperature and time of day
Supervised learning learns from examples where the correct answer is known, like a student with a teacher. Past meter readings give the correct kWh for many hours with known temperature and time; a model trained on them predicts the use for new hours.
Unsupervised: unlabelled data: inputs only; find groups or structure. Example: group smart-meter customers by their daily load profile, with no labels given
No correct answers are given; the method finds patterns by itself. Given each customer's 24 hourly readings, it can group customers with similar daily patterns (for example households, shops, night-time businesses).
Reinforcement: trial and error: actions earn rewards from an environment. Example: learn when to switch a heater on and off to hold a room at a set temperature
An agent acts, receives a reward or penalty, and learns which actions lead to good outcomes. The controller switches the heater, is rewarded when the room is close to the set temperature and penalised for energy used, and learns a good switching policy. SPM 405 covers supervised and unsupervised learning; reinforcement learning is mentioned for completeness.
Reward: a score the environment gives after each action
The reward is to reinforcement learning what the label is to supervised learning: the signal the method learns from.

title: Kernels
content:
Kernels# Example: a shaft orbit# Two probes record the shaft position; the orbit's shape tells healthy from misaligned. Two proximity probes at right angles measure the position of a rotating shaft (\(x\), \(y\) in \(\mu\)m)
Eddy-current proximity probes are standard on large turbines, compressors and pumps. Plotting \(y\) against \(x\) gives the shaft's orbit.
Healthy shaft: stays near the centre. Unbalance or rub: swings far out, in any direction
The direction depends on the moment of the reading; only the distance from the centre matters.
Data: 300 training readings, 3000 test
No straight line can do this# The kernel trick: in a bigger space the classes become separable by a straight line. The boundary should be a circle
Faults lie outside a ring, healthy readings inside. Any straight line cuts the ring in half.
Idea: add new inputs, such as \(x^2\) and \(y^2\). In the new inputs the circle \(x^2 + y^2 = r^2\) is a straight line (a hyperplane)
With inputs \(u = x^2\) and \(v = y^2\), the circle is the straight line \(u + v = r^2\).
Enlarge the feature space: a linear boundary in the enlarged space is a curved boundary in the original space
The same trick as adding \(x^2\) in Lecture 2
Symbols
\(r\) Radius of the boundary circle (\(\mu\)m). Kernels# linear \(\sum_j x_{ij}x_{kj}\) polynomial \(\bigl(1 + \sum_j x_{ij}x_{kj}\bigr)^d\) radial \(\exp\bigl(-\gamma\sum_j (x_{ij} - x_{kj})^2\bigr)\) The SVM only needs similarities between pairs of points, \(K(x_i, x_k)\). A kernel computes them directly, without building the new inputs
The SVM solution can be written using only inner products between training points (ISLP 9.3.2). Replacing the inner product by a kernel is equivalent to working in an enlarged space, possibly an infinite-dimensional one, without ever computing it.
Linear: \(\sum_jx_{ij}x_{kj}\). Polynomial: \((1 + \sum_jx_{ij}x_{kj})^d\). Radial: \(\exp(-\gamma\sum_j(x_{ij} - x_{kj})^2)\)
The linear kernel is the ordinary inner product (the support vector classifier). The polynomial kernel of degree 2 contains all products \(x_1^2\), \(x_2^2\), \(x_1x_2\). The radial kernel depends only on the distance between the two points.
An SVM with a kernel is called a support vector machine
Radial kernel: near points: similarity close to 1; far points: close to 0. Large \(\gamma\): very local, wiggly boundary
Symbols
\(K(x_i, x_k)\) Kernel: similarity of points \(i\) and \(k\). \(d\) Degree of the polynomial kernel. \(\gamma\) Width parameter of the radial kernel. Worked numbers
Radial kernel with \(\gamma = 0.1\) (the value chosen by CV), in standardised units: points at distance 1 have similarity \(e^{-0.1} = 0.90\); at distance 3, \(e^{-0.9} = 0.41\); at distance 5, \(e^{-2.5} = 0.08\).
Example: three kernels for the same pair of points# Compute \(K(\mathbf x, \mathbf x')\) for \(\mathbf x = (1, 2)\) and \(\mathbf x' = (2, 0)\) with the linear kernel \(\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf x'\), the polynomial kernel \((1 + \mathbf x\cdot\mathbf x')^2\) and the radial kernel \(\exp(-\gamma\|\mathbf x - \mathbf x'\|^2)\) with \(\gamma = 0.5\).
Solution triple-click to reveal Linear: \(1 \times 2 + 2 \times 0 = 2\). Polynomial: \((1 + 2)^2 = 9\). Radial: \(\|\mathbf x - \mathbf x'\|^2 = (1-2)^2 + (2-0)^2 = 5\), so \(K = e^{-0.5 \times 5} = 0.082\). The radial kernel is a similarity between 0 and 1: near 1 for close points, near 0 for distant ones.
Shaft orbit: the result# Method test error Logistic regression 0.375 Linear SVM 0.403 Polynomial SVM, \(d = 2\) 0.056 Radial SVM 0.060 Best possible (radius rule) 0.055 Table: logistic regression 0.375; linear SVM 0.403; polynomial SVM, \(d = 2\): 0.056; radial SVM 0.060; best possible (radius rule) 0.055
\(C\) and \(\gamma\) chosen by 10-fold CV: radial \(C = 10\), \(\gamma = 0.1\)
The grid: \(C \in \{0.1, 1, 10, 100\}\) and \(\gamma \in \{0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5\}\), 20 combinations.
Plot: black: the radial SVM boundary
A near-circle around the healthy readings.
Reading the shaft-orbit result# Linear methods are no better than guessing “healthy” (40% of readings are faults)
Guessing “healthy” always is wrong for the 40% that are faults; logistic regression (0.375) and the linear SVM (0.403) are no better.
Both kernels find a near-circle: the radial SVM's boundary has mean radius 33.5 \(\mu\)m
The best possible rule, “fault if the distance from the centre exceeds 32.6 \(\mu\)m”, has error 0.055. The SVMs are almost there
Because the classes overlap in radius (healthy up to about 35 \(\mu\)m, faults down to about 25), no rule can reach zero error.
The radial SVM uses 68 of the 300 readings as support vectors
If you know the physics, compute the radius yourself: \(r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\). Then even logistic regression works. Kernels help when you do not know the right features
Notebook question 5: logistic regression on \(r\) alone has test error 0.057, as good as the SVMs.
Beyond the slide: overfitting with \(\gamma\) Notebook question 6: \(\gamma = 5\), \(C = 100\) gives training error 0.013 but test error 0.126. A very local kernel with expensive violations wraps the boundary around individual points.

title: Recurrent networks
content:
Recurrent networks# Sequences: recurrent networks# A recurrent network reads a sequence one step at a time, carrying a memory forward. Diagram: inputs \(x_{t-3}, \dots, x_t\); hidden states connected in a chain; forecast from the last
A recurrent network reads a sequence one step at a time. Its hidden state \(h\) carries a memory of what came before, updated at every step with the same weights
\(h_t = g(Wh_{t-1} + Ux_t + b)\): the new memory depends on the old memory and the new input (ISLP 10.5). The same \(W\), \(U\), \(b\) at every step: the weights are shared along time, as a CNN shares them across space.
GRU and LSTM units have “gates” that decide what to keep and what to forget.
Symbols
\(x_t\) Input at time \(t\). \(h_t\) Hidden state (memory) at time \(t\). Example: forecasting a building's demand# The building of Lecture 5, metered every hour for 200 days. Task: from the last 24 hours, forecast the next hour
Training: first 150 days. Test: last 50 days (1200 forecasts)
\(50 \times 24 = 1200\) test hours.
Demand follows the daily pattern, the weather, and disturbances that last a few hours
Each hour's disturbance keeps 70% of the previous hour's, plus new noise (an AR(1) process).
Split by time: for forecasting, never split at random: train on the past, test on the future
A random split lets the model see hours just after the ones it predicts, which is impossible in use.
Forecasting: the result# Method test MSE (kW\(^2\)) Same hour yesterday 45.8 Linear, last 24 hours 13.7 Recurrent network (GRU) 11.6 Noise floor 9.0 Table: same hour yesterday 45.8; linear, last 24 hours 13.7; recurrent network (GRU) 11.6; noise floor 9.0
The linear model is the autoregressive model AR(24): a linear regression on the last 24 values. Noise floor: the part no forecast can predict
Plot: first 4 test days
Both models follow the daily pattern closely; the GRU follows the disturbances a little better.
The naive forecast ignores the current disturbance. The AR(24) model uses it. The GRU (929 parameters) does somewhat better still. No model can beat 9: the new noise each hour is unpredictable (notebook question 8). ISLP reaches a similar conclusion on stock-market data: RNNs help only modestly over a good linear AR model.
Worked numbers
GRU parameters: \(3 \times (16 \times 1 + 16 \times 16 + 16 + 16) = 3 \times 304 = 912\), plus the output \(16 + 1 = 17\): 929.

title: SVMs in practice
content:
SVMs in practice# More than two classes# One-versus-one: fit an SVM for every pair of \(K\) classes: \(K(K - 1)/2\) SVMs. Each votes; the class with the most votes wins. (scikit-learn's SVC does this.)
One-versus-all: fit \(K\) SVMs: each class against all the others. Choose the class whose SVM is most confident
Fault type: three classes (imbalance, misalignment, bearing wear): 3 SVMs either way
\(3 \times 2/2 = 3\) pairs; and 3 one-versus-all SVMs. With 10 classes it would be 45 against 10.
Symbols
\(K\) Number of classes. SVMs and logistic regression# Plot: hinge loss (SVM) and log loss (logistic) against \(y_if(x_i)\), the signed distance
\(y_if(x_i)\) is positive for a correctly classified point and large when it is far on the correct side. The SVM can be written as minimising the hinge loss \(\max(0, 1 - y_if(x_i))\) plus a ridge-like penalty (ISLP 9.5).
Both penalise points on the wrong side. The SVM ignores points safely outside the street (loss exactly 0)
That is why only support vectors matter. The log loss is never exactly zero, so every point has a little influence.
The name: the graph is bent like a door hinge at \(y_if(x_i) = 1\).
So the two methods usually give similar answers: 0.177 and 0.176 on dataset B
Logistic regression gives probabilities; an SVM gives a class (and a distance)
Things to watch# Standardise the inputs: kernels use distances
Tune \(C\) and \(\gamma\) together by cross-validation, over a grid
They interact: a large \(\gamma\) needs a smaller \(C\) to avoid overfitting.
Know your library's \(C\): scikit-learn's \(C\) is the opposite of ISLP's
Large datasets: kernel SVMs become slow beyond some tens of thousands of rows
Training time grows roughly with the square of the number of rows or worse.
Probabilities: SVC(probability=True) estimates them with an extra step; they are less reliable than logistic regression's
The extra step fits a sigmoid to the SVM distances using internal cross-validation (Platt scaling).
Summary# The maximal margin classifier finds the widest street between two classes Only the support vectors decide the boundary The soft margin allows overlap; \(C\) controls the width (in scikit-learn: small \(C\) = wide) Kernels give curved boundaries by enlarging the feature space implicitly SVMs and logistic regression often perform alike; kernels win when the boundary is curved Before next class# Read ISLP Chapter 9 (9.1–9.5) Run lecture06_svm.ipynb in Google Colab Group: if your output is a category, try a radial SVM (tune \(C\) and \(\gamma\) by CV) and add it to your comparison table Next class: neural networks and deep learning
ISLP Chapter 10.

title: When to use deep learning
content:
When to use deep learning# When to use deep learning# Deep learning needs graphics cards (GPUs) and a lot of data. Photo: Timothy Borkowski, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 Deep learning shines: images, sound, vibration signals, text; raw inputs where you do not know the right features; large datasets
Try simpler models first: a table of measured features (our machines: the forest won); small datasets; when you must explain the model
Occam's razor (ISLP 10.6): if a simpler model does about as well, prefer it
Today's three examples show all three cases: networks lost on a table, won decisively on images, and helped modestly on a sequence.
Predictive models: useful, within limits. xkcd #2169 “Predictive Models” by Randall Munroe, CC BY-NC 2.5. Hover for the alt text. Things to watch# Standardise the inputs (images: subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation)
Keep a validation set for early stopping and for choosing the architecture; keep the test set for the end
Randomness: results change with the seed and the library version. Fix the seed; report the spread over a few seeds
Start small: a small network that works beats a big one that does not train
Hardware: small networks run on a CPU; for large images use Colab's free GPU
In Colab: Runtime, Change runtime type, GPU; then move the model and data to "cuda".

title: Words, notation and matrix algebra
content:
Words, notation and matrix algebra# Notation# \(i\) irradiance cell temp. power \(x_{i1}\) (W/m\(^2\)) \(x_{i2}\) (\(^\circ\)C) \(y_i\) (W) 1 260 31.1 70.3 2 270 31.2 86.4 3 270 21.9 78.5 \(\vdots\) \(\vdots\) \(\vdots\) \(\vdots\) 20 950 60.4 231.4 The notation of ISLP, used in every lecture of the course. The slide's Symbols box gives each symbol in words.
Matrix \(\bX\) with entries \(x_{11}, x_{12}, \dots, x_{np}\)
All inputs in one table: \(n\) rows (observations) and \(p\) columns (inputs). Bold capital letters are matrices.
Two subscripts: the first (\(i\)) says which observation (row), the second (\(j\)) which input (column). Row \(i\) is everything we measured about observation \(i\): a list of \(p\) numbers. Together the \(y_i\) form a column of length \(n\).
Example: a solar panel: \(i\), irradiance \(x_{i1}\) (W/m\(^2\)), cell temperature \(x_{i2}\) (\(^\circ\)C), power \(y_i\) (W); rows \((260, 31.1, 70.3)\), \((270, 31.2, 86.4)\), \((270, 21.9, 78.5)\), …, \((950, 60.4, 231.4)\). Here \(n = 20\), \(p = 2\); \(x_{21} = 270\), \(y_3 = 78.5\). Irradiance: sunlight power falling on each square metre
Each row is one reading of the panel: the sunlight falling on it, its temperature, and its electrical output. 20 readings of two inputs. \(x_{21}\) is row 2, column 1: the irradiance of reading 2. \(y_3\) is the power of reading 3. This panel returns in Lecture 2.
Try it: Ask for \(x_{32}\) (21.9 \(^\circ\)C) and \(y_1\) (70.3 W).
Symbols
\(n\) Number of observations (rows). \(p\) Number of inputs (columns). \(x_{ij}\) Input \(j\) of observation \(i\). \(\bX\) Data matrix, \(n\times p\). \(x_i\) Row \(i\): all inputs of observation \(i\). \(y_i\) Output (label) of observation \(i\). Beyond the slide ISLP also writes \(x_i \in \mathbb R^p\) (“\(x_i\) is a list of \(p\) real numbers”) and uses bold \(\mathbf x_j\) for column \(j\), one input measured over all observations. These appear in later lectures.
Matrix algebra: transpose and product# Transpose: swap rows and columns, \((\bX\T)_{ij} = x_{ji}\)
The transpose turns rows into columns. An \(n\times p\) matrix becomes \(p\times n\).
Product of \(A\) (\(r\times d\)) and \(B\) (\(d\times s\)): \((AB)_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^d a_{ik}b_{kj}\), size \(r\times s\)
To get entry \((i, j)\) of the product, go along row \(i\) of \(A\) and down column \(j\) of \(B\), multiply pairs and add. The sum sign \(\sum_{k=1}^d\) is shorthand for adding the terms for \(k = 1, 2, \dots, d\).
Example: \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}5&6\\7&8\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}19&22\\43&50\end{pmatrix}\), e.g. \((AB)_{11} = 1\cdot5 + 2\cdot7 = 19\)
A worked example to do together.
Rule for sizes: \((r\times d)(d\times s) = r\times s\). The inner sizes must match
The inner sizes (\(d\) and \(d\)) must be equal, or the product is not defined; the result has the outer sizes. Checking sizes catches most coding errors.
Symbols
\(\bX\T\) Transpose of \(\bX\). \(r\times d\) A matrix with \(r\) rows and \(d\) columns. \(a_{ik}\) Entry in row \(i\), column \(k\) of \(A\). \(\sum_{k=1}^d\) Sum over \(k\) from 1 to \(d\). Worked numbers
\((AB)_{12} = 1\cdot6 + 2\cdot8 = 22\); \((AB)_{21} = 3\cdot5 + 4\cdot7 = 43\); \((AB)_{22} = 3\cdot6 + 4\cdot8 = 50\).
Why matrices? All predictions at once# A linear model predicts every observation with one product: \(\hat{\mathbf y} = \bX\boldsymbol\beta\) (\(n\) predictions \(=\) \(n\times p\) inputs times \(p\) parameters). Check the sizes: \((n\times p)(p\times 1) = n\times 1\)
A linear model multiplies each input by a parameter and adds the results. Writing the parameters as a column \(\boldsymbol\beta\), one matrix product gives the predictions for all \(n\) observations at once.
Row \(i\) of the product: \(\hat y_i = x_{i1}\beta_1 + x_{i2}\beta_2 + \dots + x_{ip}\beta_p\)
This is the product rule of slide 22 applied to row \(i\) of \(\bX\) and the single column \(\boldsymbol\beta\).
In Python (NumPy): X.T is the transpose, X @ beta the product
NumPy's notation; students meet it in the notebook.
Solar panel: \(n = 20\), \(p = 2\): a \(20\times 2\) table times 2 parameters gives 20 predicted powers
The sizes check: \((20\times 2)(2\times 1) = 20\times 1\).
Symbols
\(\boldsymbol\beta\) Beta: column of \(p\) parameters. \(\hat y_i\) Y hat: the prediction for observation \(i\). The hat means “estimated”. \(\hat{\mathbf y}\) Column of all \(n\) predictions. Example: three predictions in one product# A solar-panel model predicts power \(\hat y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 G + \beta_2 T\) from irradiance \(G\) (W/m²) and temperature \(T\) (°C), with \(\boldsymbol\beta = (2.0,\ 0.25,\ -0.3)\). Write the three readings below as a matrix \(\mathbf X\) (with a column of ones) and compute \(\hat{\mathbf y} = \mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta\).
reading \(G\) \(T\) 1 260 31.1 2 410 35.6 3 150 28.4 Solution triple-click to reveal \[ \mathbf X = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 260 & 31.1 \\ 1 & 410 & 35.6 \\ 1 & 150 & 28.4 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta = \begin{pmatrix} 2.0 + 0.25(260) - 0.3(31.1) \\ 2.0 + 0.25(410) - 0.3(35.6) \\ 2.0 + 0.25(150) - 0.3(28.4) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 57.67 \\ 93.82 \\ 30.98 \end{pmatrix}\ \mathrm{W}. \]Each row of \(\mathbf X\) times \(\boldsymbol\beta\) is one prediction: one matrix product gives them all.

title: Statistical learning
content:
Statistical learning# Two words from statistics: average and variance# The next slides use the symbols \(\mathbb E\) and \(\operatorname{Var}\). Many students last met them in a first-year statistics course, so they are defined here, with an example, before they are used.
Expected value (long-run average): \(\mathbb E(Z) \approx (z_1 + z_2 + \dots + z_m)/m\) for a large number of repeats \(m\)
A random quantity \(Z\) takes a different value each time it is measured. Its expected value is the average we would get if we measured it very many times. “Approximately” because the average of a finite number of repeats is only close to it.
Variance (spread about the average): \(\operatorname{Var}(Z) = \mathbb E(Z - \mathbb EZ)^2\)
Take each value's distance from the average, square it, and average. A large variance means the values scatter widely.
Standard deviation: \(\sigma = \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(Z)}\), in the same units as \(Z\)
The variance is in squared units (\(^\circ\)C\(^2\)); its square root, the standard deviation, is back in the units of \(Z\) and gives the typical size of the scatter.
Example: readings of a 50 \(^\circ\)C cup with noise \(\sigma = 2\) \(^\circ\)C: average 50 \(^\circ\)C, variance 4 \(^\circ\)C\(^2\)
A thermometer with random noise of standard deviation 2 \(^\circ\)C reads 49.1, 51.8, 50.6, …; the readings average to 50 \(^\circ\)C and their variance is \(2^2 = 4\) \(^\circ\)C\(^2\). The same numbers appear in the cooling-curve example (slide 33).
Symbols
\(Z\); \(z_1, z_2, \dots\) A random quantity; its measured values. \(\mathbb E\) Expected value: the average over very many repeats. \(\operatorname{Var}\) Variance: the average squared distance from the average. \(\sigma\) Sigma: standard deviation, \(\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}}\). Example: average and variance of mains voltage# Five readings of the mains voltage are 229.0, 231.5, 228.2, 232.1 and 230.2 V. Find the average, the variance (divide by \(n\)) and the standard deviation.
Solution triple-click to reveal Average: \(\bar v = (229.0 + 231.5 + 228.2 + 232.1 + 230.2)/5 = 230.20\) V.
Deviations from the average: -1.20, +1.30, -2.00, +1.90, +0.00. Squared: 1.4400, 1.6900, 4.0000, 3.6100, 0.0000.
Variance \(= (1.4400 + 1.6900 + 4.0000 + 3.6100 + 0.0000)/5 = 2.1480\) V², standard deviation \(= \sqrt{2.1480} = 1.466\) V.
Statistical learning: estimating \(f\)# Inputs \(X = (X_1, X_2, \dots, X_p)\), output \(Y\). We assume \(Y = f(X) + \varepsilon\)
The central equation of the course. The output is some function of the inputs plus random error. Machine learning is the art of estimating \(f\) from data.
Learning means finding an estimate \(\hat f\) of \(f\) from data, then predicting \(\hat Y = \hat f(X)\)
The hat means “estimated from data”. \(\hat f\) is the model.
Capital \(X\), \(Y\): the quantities in general. Small \(x_i\), \(y_i\): one measured observation
\(Y\) is “panel power” in general; \(y_3 = 78.5\) W is the power in reading 3.
\(f\) is the true relation in nature. It exists, but we do not know it. \(\varepsilon\) (epsilon) includes measurement noise and everything we did not measure. “Unrelated to \(X\)” (independent): the noise does not depend on the inputs. “Average zero”: it is as likely to be positive as negative, so \(\mathbb E(\varepsilon) = 0\).
Solar panel: \(X_1\) = irradiance, \(X_2\) = cell temperature, \(Y\) = power. \(\varepsilon\): measurement noise and effects we did not measure (dust, wind). No model can predict it from \(X\)
For the solar panel, dust on the glass or wind cooling it change the power, but we did not measure them, so their effect is part of the noise.
Symbols
\(X\), \(X_j\) Inputs; \(X_j\) is the \(j\)-th input. \(Y\) Output. \(f\) True, unknown relation between \(X\) and \(Y\). \(\varepsilon\) Epsilon: random error, mean zero. \(\hat f\), \(\hat Y\) Estimated function and its prediction. Reducible and irreducible error# The average squared prediction error splits into two parts: \(\mathbb E(Y - \hat Y)^2 = [f(X) - \hat f(X)]^2 + \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)\): reducible + irreducible
The left side is the average, over many new observations, of (measured \(-\) predicted)\(^2\).
Reducible: our \(\hat f\) is not the true \(f\). A better method or more data can shrink it
\([f - \hat f]^2\) comes from our estimate being imperfect.
Irreducible: the noise \(\varepsilon\) itself. No method can remove it
\(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) = \sigma^2\) is the noise; it is not predictable from \(X\).
Key idea: even the perfect model, \(\hat f = f\), has average squared error \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)\)
Put \(\hat f = f\) in the equation: the first term is zero and only the noise remains. This sets a floor that no model can go below; we see it in the data on slide 34.
Symbols
\(\mathbb E(Y - \hat Y)^2\) Average squared prediction error. \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)\) Variance of the noise, \(\sigma^2\). Beyond the slide: where the equation comes from With \(Y = f(X) + \varepsilon\) and \(\hat Y = \hat f(X)\) for a fixed \(X\): \(\mathbb E(Y - \hat Y)^2 = \mathbb E(f - \hat f + \varepsilon)^2 = (f - \hat f)^2 + 2(f - \hat f)\mathbb E(\varepsilon) + \mathbb E(\varepsilon^2)\). The middle term is zero because \(\mathbb E(\varepsilon) = 0\), and \(\mathbb E(\varepsilon^2) = \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)\).
Why estimate \(f\)? Prediction and inference# Prediction: we want accurate predictions \(\hat Y\). How \(\hat f\) works inside does not matter: it can be a black box. Example: forecast tomorrow's panel output for the grid operator
If we only need good predictions, it does not matter how \(\hat f\) works inside. A “black box” is a model whose inner workings we do not look at.
Inference: we want to understand how \(Y\) depends on each input \(X_j\). \(\hat f\) must be simple enough to read. Example: how much power is lost per degree of heating? (Lecture 2)
If we want understanding, \(\hat f\) must be interpretable. Solar cells lose efficiency as they heat up; a simple model of the panel gives this loss as one parameter, answered in Lecture 2.
Parametric and non-parametric methods# A parametric method fixes the form of f and learns a few numbers; a non-parametric method lets the data decide the shape. Parametric: 1. Assume a form for \(f\), e.g. linear: \(f(X) = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 + \dots + \beta_pX_p\). 2. Fit it: estimate \(\beta_0, \dots, \beta_p\) from data
A parametric method first chooses a formula with a fixed number of unknown parameters, then estimates them. Learning \(f\) becomes learning a few numbers.
\(+\) only \(p + 1\) numbers to estimate; \(-\) if the assumed form is wrong, the fit is poor
Few parameters need little data and are easy to interpret. But if nature is not linear, no choice of the \(\beta\)'s fixes that.
Non-parametric: assume no fixed form; follow the data as closely as is reasonable. Examples: \(K\)-nearest neighbours (later today), decision trees (Lecture 5)
These methods let the data decide the shape of \(f\).
\(+\) can fit many shapes of \(f\); \(-\) needs many more observations; \(-\) harder to interpret; can follow the noise
Flexibility is powerful but costly: more data are needed, and the model may fit the noise (overfitting, slide 34).
Symbols
\(\beta_0, \dots, \beta_p\) Beta nought, beta one, …: the parameters. \(\beta_0\) is \(f\) when all inputs are zero; \(\beta_j\) is the change in \(f\) per unit of \(X_j\). Physics gives us parametric forms# Physics often tells us the form of f: exponential decay, Newton's law of cooling. Machine learning then only has to find the numbers. Newton's law of cooling: \(T(t) = T_{\mathrm{env}} + (T_0 - T_{\mathrm{env}})\,e^{-kt}\). Three parameters: \(T_{\mathrm{env}}\), \(T_0\), \(k\)
Physics often supplies the right formula. Newton's law of cooling has three parameters: the surrounding temperature \(T_{\mathrm{env}}\), the starting temperature \(T_0\), and the cooling rate \(k\). At \(t = 0\), \(e^0 = 1\) and \(T = T_0\); as \(t\) grows, \(e^{-kt} \to 0\) and \(T \to T_{\mathrm{env}}\).
Key idea: know the law? Fit its parameters. No law? A flexible method may do better
With the right law, a parametric fit is best: three numbers, each with a physical meaning. Without one, a flexible method may win. The cooling cup returns on slide 33, fitted without the law.
Symbols
\(T(t)\) Temperature at time \(t\) (\(^\circ\)C). \(t\) Time since the start (min). \(T_{\mathrm{env}}\) Temperature of the surroundings. \(T_0\) Temperature at \(t = 0\). \(k\) Cooling rate constant (per min). \(e^{-kt}\) Exponential decay from 1 towards 0. Flexibility versus interpretability# Chart: methods placed by flexibility (horizontal) and interpretability (vertical): subset selection, lasso, least squares (top left); generalised additive models, trees (middle); bagging, boosting, support vector machines, deep learning (bottom right)
The chart, from ISLP, shows a trade-off. Methods at the top left are simple and easy to interpret but can only fit simple shapes. Methods at the bottom right can fit almost anything but are hard to interpret.
Flexibility: how many shapes of \(f\) a method can fit. Interpretability: how easily we can read what the model has learned
A straight line is inflexible but easy to read: its slope is one number with a meaning. A deep network can fit almost any shape, but its millions of parameters have no individual meaning.
The names are only labels for now; each method comes in Lectures 2–7
Least squares and subset selection: Lectures 2 and 4; lasso: Lecture 4; additive models and trees: Lecture 5; support vector machines: Lecture 6; deep learning: Lecture 7. Students do not need to know them yet.
Inference: choose a less flexible model. Each parameter has a meaning you can check against physics
If the aim is understanding, use a simple model whose parameters have physical meaning.
Prediction: a more flexible model may help, but not always: very flexible models can overfit, following the noise instead of \(f\)
Even for prediction, more flexibility is not automatically better. This is the subject of slides 33–36.
Supervised vs. unsupervised; regression vs. classification# Regression predicts a number; classification predicts a category. Supervised: each \(x_i\) has a label \(y_i\). Goal: predict \(y\) for new \(x\), or understand how \(y\) depends on \(x\). Linear and logistic regression, SVMs, boosting, neural networks
As on slide 20, now in symbols.
Unsupervised: no \(y_i\). Goal: find groups or structure in the \(x_i\). Clustering, principal component analysis (PCA): Lecture 8
Clustering finds groups; PCA finds the few combinations of inputs that carry most of the variation.
Regression: \(y\) is quantitative (a number). Electricity use (kWh) of an area; the true temperature from a drifting sensor's reading
The output is a number on a scale. Correcting a drifting sensor is a regression: from its raw reading (and perhaps its age and the ambient temperature) predict the true value measured by a reference instrument.
Classification: \(y\) is qualitative (a category, also called a class). Healthy or faulty machine; adulterated or pure milk
The output is a label from a fixed list. Milk adulteration was named in the survey: from measured properties (density, conductivity, spectrum) decide whether a sample is pure.
The boundary can blur: logistic regression predicts a class probability, which is a number
Logistic regression (Lecture 3) is a classification method, yet its output is a probability, which is a number.

title: Assessing model accuracy
content:
Assessing model accuracy# Measuring the quality of fit: the mean squared error# The residual of each point is the vertical distance to the fitted line. The mean of their squares is the MSE. Mean squared error on the training data: \(\mathrm{MSE} = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat f(x_i))^2\)
The standard score for a regression model.
In words: for each observation, measured minus predicted, squared; then the average
Read the formula from the inside out: \(\hat f(x_i)\) is the prediction, \(y_i - \hat f(x_i)\) the error, the square makes it positive, and \(\frac1n\sum\) averages over the observations.
Small MSE: predictions close to the data. Squaring makes every error positive and punishes large errors most
Without squaring, positive and negative errors would cancel. An error of 3 counts 9 times as much as an error of 1.
Example: errors \(+1\), \(-2\), \(+3\) \(^\circ\)C: \(\mathrm{MSE} = (1 + 4 + 9)/3 \approx 4.7\) \(^\circ\)C\(^2\)
Worked numbers
\(1^2 = 1\), \((-2)^2 = 4\), \(3^2 = 9\); sum 14; divided by \(n = 3\) gives 4.67 \(^\circ\)C\(^2\).
Symbols
\(y_i\) Measured output of observation \(i\). \(\hat f(x_i)\) The model's prediction for observation \(i\). \(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\) Average over the \(n\) observations. MSE Mean squared error. Units of \(y\) squared (\(^\circ\)C\(^2\)). Example: the mean squared error by hand# A model predicts the temperature of a motor housing at five times. The measured and predicted values (°C) are
measured \(y_i\) 20.1 22.4 25.0 27.9 30.2 predicted \(\hat y_i\) 20.5 22.0 25.6 27.5 30.0 Compute the mean squared error and its square root (the RMSE). What are the units of each?
Solution triple-click to reveal Residuals \(y_i - \hat y_i\): -0.4, +0.4, -0.6, +0.4, +0.2. Their squares: 0.16, 0.16, 0.36, 0.16, 0.04.
\[ \mathrm{MSE} = \frac{1}{5}(0.16 + 0.16 + 0.36 + 0.16 + 0.04) = 0.176\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}^2, \qquad \mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{0.176} = 0.420\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}. \]The MSE is in squared units; the RMSE is back in °C, so it reads as a typical error of about 0.420 °C.
Example: fitting a cooling curve# A hot drink cools towards room temperature: a curve we know from physics. Photo: epSos.de, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0 15 readings from a temperature sensor in a cooling cup of tea (simulated, noise \(\sigma = 2\) \(^\circ\)C), fitted with polynomials \(\hat T = a_0 + a_1t + a_2t^2 + \dots + a_dt^d\). The degree \(d\) is the highest power: a higher degree is a more flexible curve
The data follow Newton's law of cooling (slide 29), \(T = 25 + 60\,e^{-t/8}\) \(^\circ\)C, plus random noise with standard deviation 2 \(^\circ\)C. We pretend not to know the law and fit polynomials instead. A polynomial of degree \(d\) has \(d + 1\) parameters \(a_0, \dots, a_d\); more parameters give a more flexible curve.
Plots: degree 1 (straight line), degree 3, degree 12
Degree 1 (a straight line) is too stiff: it misses the curve. Degree 3 follows the cooling curve well. Degree 12 passes very close to every point, but wiggles wildly between them, especially near the end.
Which fit would you trust to predict the temperature at \(t = 26\) min?
Degree 12 has the smallest training MSE, but near 26 minutes it swings to over 70 \(^\circ\)C, which is physically absurd for a cooling cup. Degree 3 is the sensible choice. The next slide makes this precise.
Symbols
\(\hat T\) Predicted temperature. \(a_0, \dots, a_d\) The parameters of the polynomial. \(d\) Degree: the highest power of \(t\). \(\sigma\) Standard deviation of the noise (here 2 \(^\circ\)C). Training MSE versus test MSE# Keep some data aside: fit on the training data, judge on the test data. Too simple, just right, too flexible. Training MSE: on the 15 readings used to fit. Test MSE: on 1000 new readings
We fit each polynomial to the 15 training readings, and then measure its MSE both on those same readings (training MSE) and on 1000 new readings it never saw (test MSE).
Plot: training MSE and test MSE against flexibility (polynomial degree 1–12), log scale, with \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) = 4\)
The vertical axis is logarithmic: each gridline is ten times the one below, so values from 0.7 to 300 fit on one plot.
Training MSE always falls as flexibility grows
A more flexible model can always get at least as close to the training points: from 71 at degree 1 down to 0.7 at degree 12.
Test MSE falls, then rises: a U-shape
At first more flexibility captures the real curve better and the test MSE falls (46 at degree 1, 5.0 at degree 3). Beyond that, the extra flexibility fits the noise in the 15 training points, which does not repeat in new data, so the test MSE rises (168 at degree 12).
Test MSE never goes below \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) = 2^2 = 4\)
The irreducible error of slide 26. Even the true curve would have test MSE 4 (green line). The best model, degree 3, gets to 5.0, close to this floor.
Small training MSE with large test MSE is overfitting
Degree 12: training MSE 0.7 (below the noise level!) but test MSE 168. A training MSE below the noise variance is a warning sign that the model is memorising noise.
Key idea: choose the model by its test error
The most important rule of machine learning. Lecture 4 shows how to estimate the test error when there is no separate test set (cross-validation).
Symbols
Training MSE MSE on the data used to fit the model. Test MSE MSE on new data not used in fitting. \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)\) Noise variance: here \(2^2 = 4\) \(^\circ\)C\(^2\). Worked numbers
From the plot: degree 1: training 71.3, test 45.6; degree 3: training 2.5, test 5.0; degree 12: training 0.70, test 168.
The bias–variance decomposition# Bias: how far the average model is from the truth. Variance: how much the model changes from one data set to another. As flexibility grows, bias falls and variance rises; the test error is lowest in between. Imagine repeating the experiment many times, each with a new training set, and predicting at the same new input \(x_0\)
Each repeat gives a different set of 15 noisy readings, so a different fitted curve, so a different prediction at \(x_0\). The expected value \(\mathbb E\) averages over all these repeats (slide 24).
\(\mathbb E(y_0 - \hat f(x_0))^2 = \operatorname{Var}(\hat f(x_0)) + [\operatorname{Bias}(\hat f(x_0))]^2 + \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)\)
The average squared error at \(x_0\) splits into three parts, all positive. This explains the U-shape of the test MSE.
Variance: how much the prediction changes from one training set to another
A very flexible model follows every detail of its training data, so different training sets give very different curves: high variance.
Bias: average prediction minus the true \(f(x_0)\); the error from using a model that is too simple
A straight line cannot follow a curved cooling law, however much data it has: its average prediction is systematically off. That systematic error is the bias.
\(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)\): the noise: the irreducible error, as before
As on slide 26.
Symbols
\(x_0\), \(y_0\) A new input and its (noisy) output. \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat f(x_0))\) Variance of the prediction over different training sets. \(\operatorname{Bias}(\hat f(x_0))\) Average prediction minus the true \(f(x_0)\). Try it. Raise the polynomial degree. The training error always falls; the test error falls, then rises again: first bias goes down, then variance takes over. Underfitting and overfitting# Sketch: bias\(^2\) falls and variance rises with flexibility; their sum plus \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)\) is the U-shaped test MSE
The curves are drawn by hand to show the shapes, not computed from data. The noise line is flat: flexibility does not change it.
High bias, low variance \(\Rightarrow\) underfitting: too simple to follow \(f\) (the straight line on the cooling data)
Stable but wrong.
Low bias, high variance \(\Rightarrow\) overfitting: follows the noise (degree 12)
Right on average, but unstable: each training set gives a wildly different curve.
More flexibility lowers bias but raises variance. The best model balances the two: the bottom of the U
As flexibility grows, bias falls and variance rises; their sum is smallest in between. That is the bottom of the U. The noise term cannot be reduced.

title: Classification
content:
Classification# Classification: the error rate# A portable vibration-measurement kit. Vibration levels are the inputs of our machine-fault examples. Photo: NotecA, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 For categories the MSE makes no sense. Count the mistakes instead
“Faulty minus healthy” has no meaning, so we cannot square a difference.
Error rate (fraction of wrong labels): \(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n I(y_i \neq \hat y_i)\)
\(I(\cdot)\) is the indicator function: 1 if the statement in brackets is true, 0 if false. For each observation it gives 1 for a wrong label, 0 for a right one; adding them counts the mistakes, and dividing by \(n\) gives the fraction.
As with the MSE, we care about the test error rate
The error on new data is what matters.
Example: 10 motors; the model labels 2 of them wrongly. Error rate \(= 2/10 = 0.2\). Accuracy \(= 1 - 0.2 = 0.8\)
The accuracy (fraction correct) of slide 18 is one minus the error rate.
Symbols
\(\hat y_i\) Predicted class of observation \(i\). \(\neq\) Is not equal to. \(I(\cdot)\) Indicator: 1 if the statement is true, 0 if false. The Bayes classifier# Assign the input \(x_0\) to the class \(j\) with the largest \(\Pr(Y = j \mid X = x_0)\)
For each input, pick the class that is most probable for that input. The vertical bar is read “given”.
It has the lowest possible error rate (the Bayes error rate)
No classifier can do better, because it always picks the most probable class.
But we never know these probabilities in practice: it is an ideal, not a method
The true probabilities are unknown, so it is an ideal to approach. In the notebook the data are simulated, so the Bayes classifier is known and we can compare against it.
Example: a motor vibrates at 6 mm/s. Suppose \(\Pr(\text{faulty} \mid 6\text{ mm/s}) = 0.8\) and \(\Pr(\text{healthy} \mid 6\text{ mm/s}) = 0.2\). The Bayes classifier says faulty
Of all motors that vibrate at 6 mm/s, 80% are faulty. Labelling them all faulty is wrong 20% of the time, and no rule can do better at that vibration level.
The Bayes error rate plays the role of the irreducible error: no classifier can beat it
The classification version of \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)\) on slide 26.
Symbols
\(j\) A class label. \(\Pr(Y = j \mid X = x_0)\) Probability that the class is \(j\), given input \(x_0\). \(K\)-nearest neighbours (KNN)# KNN: find the K closest known machines and take a vote. The answer can depend on K. Find the \(K\) training points closest to \(x_0\), then estimate \(\Pr(Y = j \mid X = x_0) \approx \frac1K\sum_{i\in\mathcal N_0} I(y_i = j)\) and choose the most common class
KNN estimates the unknown probabilities from the neighbours: the probability of class \(j\) is the fraction of the \(K\) nearest training points that belong to class \(j\). Then it picks the most common class.
Small \(K\) (1 or 3): flexible, noisy boundary \(\Rightarrow\) may overfit
With \(K = 1\), each new point takes the label of its single nearest neighbour; the boundary follows every noisy point. The training error is zero, but the test error is not.
Large \(K\): smooth boundary \(\Rightarrow\) may underfit
With a very large \(K\), the vote is taken over a wide region and the boundary becomes too smooth to follow the real shape. \(K\) plays the same role as the polynomial degree on slide 34, in reverse: small \(K\) is flexible.
Example: \(K = 5\): 4 of the 5 nearest motors are faulty, so \(\Pr(\text{faulty}) \approx 4/5 = 0.8\): label faulty
The indicator is 1 for the four faulty neighbours and 0 for the healthy one; the sum is 4 and \(\frac1K = \frac15\).
KNN is non-parametric: it keeps the training data and assumes no formula for \(f\)
As on slide 28.
Symbols
\(K\) Number of neighbours used by KNN. \(\mathcal N_0\) The set of the \(K\) training points nearest to \(x_0\). \(i \in \mathcal N_0\) \(i\) is one of those neighbours. Try it. Change \(K\). With \(K = 1\) the training error is 0 but the test error is high; a moderate \(K\) gives the lowest test error. Example: KNN by hand# Six machines have vibration levels (mm/s) and known states:
vibration 1.0 1.5 2.2 3.0 3.8 4.5 state healthy healthy faulty healthy faulty faulty Classify a new machine with vibration 2.5 mm/s using KNN with \(K = 1\) and with \(K = 3\).
Solution triple-click to reveal Distances from 2.5: 1 → 1.5, 1.5 → 1.0, 2.2 → 0.3, 3 → 0.5, 3.8 → 1.3, 4.5 → 2.0.
\(K = 1\): the nearest machine is at 2.2 (distance 0.3), which is faulty, so predict faulty. \(K = 3\): the three nearest are at 2.2, 3, 1.5: faulty, healthy, healthy. The majority is healthy. The prediction can change with \(K\): that is why \(K\) is chosen by checking the error on new data.
Summary# Machine learning learns rules (a model) from data with known answers
Every method has three parts: representation, evaluation, optimisation
We assume \(Y = f(X) + \varepsilon\) and estimate \(f\); the noise \(\varepsilon\) cannot be removed
Judge a model by its test error. Too simple underfits (high bias); too flexible overfits (high variance)
Classification uses the error rate; KNN estimates class probabilities from the \(K\) nearest neighbours
These five points are what students should take from the lecture; each returns in every later lecture.
Before next class# Read ISLP Chapter 2 (Statistical Learning) It covers everything in the second half of today's lecture.
Run lecture01_intro_ml.ipynb in Google Colab: reproduce the training and test MSE curves, then classify healthy and faulty machines with KNN for different values of \(K\) The notebook reproduces slides 33–39 and asks questions about them.
